When you’re shopping online, saved card details mean you don’t have to leave the checkout page to find your wallet.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Samsung Electronics, SK hynix, and Micron are reportedly working together to develop common charging standards for mobile robots used in semiconductor fabrication plants, according to a fresh report.
  • According to a report by Seoul Economic Daily, the initiative aims to establish common technical specifications that would allow robots from different manufacturers to share charging equipment, reducing the cost and complexity of deploying large robotic fleets across semiconductor manufacturing facilities.
  • According to recent reports, so why are three of the world's biggest memory manufacturers, who are also competitors, coming together to establish standards for the robotics industry?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Samsung Electronics, SK hynix, and Micron are reportedly working together to develop common charging standards for mobile robots used in semiconductor fabrication plants, according to a fresh report. Representatives from the three companies have reportedly formed an early-stage consultative body to lead standardization efforts, alongside major industry stakeholders such as the Semiconductor Equipment and Materials International (SEMI) industry association.

According to a report by Seoul Economic Daily, the initiative aims to establish common technical specifications that would allow robots from different manufacturers to share charging equipment, reducing the cost and complexity of deploying large robotic fleets across semiconductor manufacturing facilities. The broader goal is to accelerate factory automation, particularly in older fabs, while laying the groundwork for fully autonomous semiconductor manufacturing.

According to recent reports, so why are three of the world's biggest memory manufacturers, who are also competitors, coming together to establish standards for the robotics industry? What exactly does the collaboration involve? And what are the implications of something as seemingly minor as robot charging for the broader semiconductor and robotics industries?

Soaring demand for semiconductor memory chips used in AI infrastructure has driven manufacturers to automate as many production processes as possible to optimize manufacturing speed and capacity in existing facilities to increase output, while they build additional fabs. Modern semiconductor fabs already have extensive automation systems. However, even these facilities still require human workers for certain operations, such as moving materials between floors and unpacking products, that existing automation systems cannot perform. The matter is even more pronounced in older fabs, which generally have fewer automated material-handling systems and still rely on workers to move wafer containers using manual carts.

One potential solution is to hand these remaining manual operations over to mobile robots, allowing manufacturers to automate tasks without undertaking extensive renovations or installing complex fixed transport systems. These could include autonomous mobile robots (AMRs) that transport materials around the factory, mobile manipulators that combine robotic arms with moving platforms, and humanoid robots capable of performing more complicated handling tasks.

Recent findings suggest that the problem, however, is that these robots come in different builds and configurations, often with their own batteries and accompanying charging infrastructure. A semiconductor fab deploying multiple robot models from different manufacturers could consequently end up requiring separate charging stations for each model. In addition to increasing equipment and maintenance costs, these installations consume valuable factory floor space.

The proposed initiative seeks to address this problem by establishing common charging specifications that different robot manufacturers can adopt. Standardized charging infrastructure would allow multiple types of robots to use compatible charging stations, reducing the need for separate installations and making it easier for semiconductor manufacturers to expand their robotic fleets without adding operational inefficiencies.

The alliance is considering standards covering battery specifications for different mobile robots, charging-station equipment and communication protocols, charging connectors, and battery management systems (BMS). Together, these specifications would establish common requirements for the physical and electronic interfaces involved in charging robots inside semiconductor fabs.

According to recent reports, the initial objective is to achieve charging compatibility across different robot models. In addition to letting a fab deploy robots from several manufacturers without having to install a separate charging system for every model, this would also give manufacturers greater flexibility when purchasing newly introduced robots, since their choice of supplier would no longer be as heavily influenced by the charging infrastructure already installed in the facility.

A subsequent step would involve integrating robot charging data with the fab's manufacturing execution system (MES), the software that coordinates and monitors manufacturing operations. With access to information such as battery charge levels, robot availability, and production schedules, the system could coordinate when individual robots operate and when they return for charging. For example, robots could be scheduled to recharge during periods of lower demand or while other robots handle critical material transfers, minimizing interruptions to production. This integration would become increasingly important as manufacturers deploy larger fleets of robots across the hundreds of individual processes involved in semiconductor fabrication.

Interestingly, the three chipmakers leading the standardization efforts are primarily customers of industrial robotics manufacturers, not manufacturers of the robots themselves, except for Samsung, which has an established robotics business. The objective is to develop specifications that robotics manufacturers and charging-equipment suppliers can incorporate into their products.

On the other hand, the three companies are not independently creating specifications and dictating them to suppliers. The initiative would likely follow an industry standardization process in which robotics manufacturers, equipment suppliers, and other stakeholders contribute to developing and validating the technical requirements. For now, the project remains in its early stages, with participants still determining which components and interfaces should be standardized and consulting robotics and smart-factory specialists.

Recent findings suggest that according to DigiTimes, semiconductor industry participants first explored establishing common robotics standards roughly a decade ago, but discussions made little progress until recently. The renewed momentum is largely attributed to the ongoing semiconductor boom, which has coincided with rapid advancements in industrial robotics.

In a recent development, unprecedented demand for AI-related memory products, along with record financial performance, has given semiconductor manufacturers both the incentive and the financial resources to invest more aggressively in factory automation. While manufacturers are expanding production capacity to meet demand, newly introduced fabs take years to construct and bring online. As a result, they are simultaneously looking to squeeze out as much capacity as possible from existing facilities by increasing automation and improving productivity.

Recent findings suggest that as for why Samsung, SK hynix, and Micron are collaborating despite their intense rivalry, the answer likely comes down to shared commercial interests. Incompatible robot charging infrastructure is an industry-wide problem, and all three companies stand to benefit from a common solution. The AI boom has already encouraged numerous partnerships across the semiconductor supply chain, including between companies that are considered fierce rivals, as manufacturers look for ways to overcome common production and infrastructure constraints.

The involvement of these particular companies also gives the initiative considerable weight. Together, Samsung, SK hynix, and Micron control almost the entire global DRAM market. They also operate extensive semiconductor manufacturing networks and represent a substantial potential market for fab-specific robotic equipment. A common set of specifications backed by all three would therefore provide robotics manufacturers with a strong commercial incentive to develop compatible products, potentially shortening development cycles and accelerating adoption.

It has been revealed that although the current collaboration focuses on a relatively small aspect of factory automation, it is a significant step for broader standardization across the semiconductor manufacturing and industrial robotics industries. Common charging infrastructure would make it easier to deploy and manage mixed robotic fleets, while future integration with production management systems could bring fabs closer to operating with minimal human intervention. This longer-term ambition of completely autonomous facilities is already taking shape. Both SK hynix and Samsung have outlined looks to develop an autonomous semiconductor fab by 2030.

Google has been at its gradient redesign schtick for a while now to varying levels of success, but its latest redesign has just landed on the Pixel Watch for the Media Controls app, and I love it.

Quietly rolled out, the Media Controls app on Pixel Watch has picked up a redesign to its app icon, adopting the same gradient look we’ve seen across several other Pixel Watch apps.

The difference here is that Google’s styling expands beyond a simple coat of paint. The fresh look extends to the edge of the icon with play/pause in the center and a ring indicating playback around the border, just like the actual app itself – the app, to be clear, hasn’t been redesigned.

I’ve personally been a bit mixed on these redesigns, but this one really nails it in my book. I wish Google would do this sort of thing more often. The white borders are nice in some cases, but I very much miss the whimsy of the icons that took up the full size available to them – that mid-2010’s icon was the absolute peak in my opinion.

Pixel Watch has been quietly rolling out more of these icon redesigns in recent months, with the other most recent additions including Alarm, Stopwatch, and Timer from around August/September.

#46841. Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas is GTA 5 without the finesse - so why is the 2004 classic such a strange delight to return to?

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1333 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Eurogamer ↗ Open Full Page

Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas is GTA 5 without the finesse - so why is the 2004 classic such a strange delight to return to?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1333 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eurogamer

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that there is a place in Whitewood Estates where a promising stretch of blacktop suddenly gives way to the desert.
  • Recent findings suggest that it's fitting I guess that GTA San Andreas is such a strange delight to return to.
  • I mainly think of San Andreas these days through the lens of GTA 5, which gives you LA and its surroundings but lets the single city serve as the star.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that there is a place in Whitewood Estates where a promising stretch of blacktop suddenly gives way to the desert. It feels like the road has been erased, a sentence left unfinished. It's quietly strange, a weird bit of urban wrongfooting. But I guess it makes some kind of sense. California, after all, is home to California City, a town that was planned and then never really built. It sits out there now, north of Los Angeles, streets laid out but slowly being eaten by the sand and dirt. Still, 14,000 people lived there as of 2018. Design limitation or something stranger, this digital dead end is a reminder that all of this land, so modern, so ancient - all of this is spook country.

Recent findings suggest that it's fitting I guess that GTA San Andreas is such a strange delight to return to. As I've waited, like everyone else, for GTA 6, I've been back here in the GTA games of the past, via the slightly dodgy remasters from a few years ago. And what's come through for me, spending a few idle mornings messing around in San Andreas, a game I thought I knew pretty well, is how beautifully odd everything is now. The best part of 20 years have given a game that once strained against its host technology a genuine aesthetic. Surprisingly sparse in detailing, as angular and sheer as dream architecture, in love with expanses, San Andreas is perfectly placed, it seems to me, to capture just how weird California can be.

California and Nevada. This is the part I always forget. I mainly think of San Andreas these days through the lens of GTA 5, which gives you LA and its surroundings but lets the single city serve as the star. It has a bigger footprint than the earlier game, sure, but it uses that space to go deep on the detailing and the sense of a singular, fiercely specific place. San Andreas meanwhile offers three cities - and one of them isn't actually in California. Alongside spins on LA and San Francisco, you get a version of Las Vegas. It's quite neat really: the three points of some arcane spiritual triangle. The kind of thing Marvel Whiteside Parsons, aerospace engineer and Actual Wizard, might have scratched in the dust of his backyard to help him control the weather. He lived - and died - in Pasadena, so all this would have been familiar anyway.

There is a classic moment in every GTA. A moment where the map opens up in the early games, or when you explore enough in the later games, and simply get to understand the audacity of what is being attempted here. In San Andreas, and this feels apt, the best way to have this moment is to break the rules, sneaking into the open map before the game is fully ready for you. An early mission allows you to step away from the critical path, as it were, and peg it to the airport in Los Santos, where a plane is waiting to be pinched. Taxi, feel the thrust, and you're off. LA beneath you - sorry, Los Santos - and on the horizon a dinkytown version of the Golden Gate Bridge and the MGM Grand.

Industry observers note that dinkytown is the word. From the sky, the huge map of San Andreas, which still feels like an incredible piece of work - such ambition! - can look like toys laid out on a duvet in the remasters. Coming back from GTA 5, a masterpiece of texture, the cities of San Andreas in particular feel very weird - cramped and condensed and wonderfully stagey, arranged the way a kid might jury-rig them together from shoeboxes and stray cardboard. On your way out of Grove Street early on you pass the Los Santos equivalent of the Hollywood sign, looming so close the way it does in the movies but not in the actual city and you feel you could touch it. Downtown is reduced to a handful of the best buildings - it's always pleasing to see the one from the brilliant first act of Speed made the cut - but still manages to capture the vital stuff too, which in this case is the way that modern LA looms somewhat cruelly over the old city, captured with a strange sepulchral dignity in the form of the City Hall, so easy to spot but now so small!

Recent findings suggest that elsewhere, the ersatz Las Vega Strip looks like a drawing based on memory - a few of the classic shapes are there, but it's a sketch of a place. In this way, I guess, it captures a truth about Las Vegas. Also, perhaps, it's an admission that this is a town comfortably out of the reach of satire. As for San Francisco, it's a 60s cop movie delight to fishtail around. It nails the hills and what more do you need for a game with cars in it?

Taken as a whole these cities feel mesmerising now. And it's the limitations that make them sing, I think: those sheer granite canyons of downtown LA with its towering blocks of architecture and surprisingly thin traffic, with only the very faintest of ambient soundtracks that ensures any gunfire will pop and clap and shake you out of your seat. (Remember, I am playing the remasters and sound effects may be missing.) This is the LA of Repo Man rather than Heat - an otherland where the buildings feel alien, even the air feels alien. At night, palm trees stand out against a sky that glows a deep, clean red. GTA 5 would finesse all of this, the skyboxes and whatnot, but perhaps in that finessing something is lost. (Both games, incidentally, have such a talent for capturing California's kitsch excess that they perhaps miss some of the sweeter truths, such as the astonishing diversity of cultures a city like Los Angeles finds homes for. But how could any game do that justice?).

Dinkytowns aside, what San Andreas does better than GTA 5 is space - the peculiar flat spaces of Southern California in particular, a state in which you can never quite tell where the wilderness ends and the landscaping begins, and where the ancient rocks that announce the horizon can look new, like stage settings, while the freeways feel truly ancient, concrete lizards sleeping on the dirt, bleached by the easy sun. I can lose hours out here. I have had to double- and triple-check that GTA 5 is the bigger game, in fact, because San Andreas still feels absolutely enormous, a trick that works even when you can see the not-Golden Gate Bridge seconds after taking off from not-LAX. Grab a bike and you can spend an absolute age exploring the between-spaces which video game California and real California are both so good at conjuring, stumbling on little towns you will never stumble on again, passing commercial follies, listening as the radio pumps out "All My Exes Live in Texas".

Sources indicate that and, paradoxically, the more I play the more I realise San Andreas is very good at the little things in its own odd way. GTA 5 is an astonishing feat of seeing and transposing, but I don't think it has anything across its acres to match the sense of place offered by San Andreas' take on Grove Street, where the story begins. It's just a neighborhood, but as you cross its small space and recross it in the game's opening hours, learning how to eat food and buy clothes and get a haircut and spray paint on walls and all that jazz, the sense that this is your home is grooved and regrooved into the experience. Maybe this is why it's such a thrill to return to this earlier pass at Los Santos. Because this one is where you truly live.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Rockstar Games developer states he and his colleagues are worried about losing their jobs after GTA 6, despite the successful launch.

The long-awaited sequel arrived on November 19 to rave reviews, after racking up well over $1 billion in pre-orders, and is likely to be one of, if not the biggest, video game releases ever.

GTA 5 sold more than 230 million copies, and Rockstar animation programmer Nestor Uriarte says the follow-up is expected to surpass it.

But for some of the people who made it, launch week also brings questions about what happens in the weeks and months that follow.

According to recent reports, uriarte, who works at Rockstar’s Edinburgh studio, raised those concerns in an opinion piece for The Guardian. He described the pressure game developers have come to expect on either side of a major launch.

“While the highs of a game release like this can be incredible, game workers have also come to expect other, less welcome side effects: intense overtime in the buildup and mass redundancies in the aftermath,” Uriarte wrote.

He pointed to job losses across the games industry to explain why those fears persist, even at Rockstar.

“It indicates a lot about the industry that even my colleagues and I, working on the biggest game of all time, are worried about getting laid off. But the truth is that workers across the sector are helpless to resist the waves of redundancies crashing around us, until we get organised.”.

It has been revealed that as a result, Uriarte mentioned he was voting in favor of union recognition because he wants staff to have a say in pay, bonuses, and working conditions. He said Rockstar has already introduced some overtime pay and wants to build on that so workers are paid for every hour they put in.

Rockstar Games could strike before GTA 6 rolls out over unionization.

GTA 6 devs demand no more ‘crunch’ from Rockstar over unionization.

Rockstar Games fires dozens of devs for “gross misconduct”.

He went on to admit that there has been no suggestion from Rockstar that layoffs are imminent, but that the fears are still there among staff.

“After the big day, we have had no indication that layoffs are coming, but it’s hard not to worry about what the future holds,” he added.

#46838. Industry News: As blockbuster game releases run scared from GTA 6, meet the brave devs tackling Rockstar's behemoth head-on

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1259 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Eurogamer ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: As blockbuster game releases run scared from GTA 6, meet the brave devs tackling Rockstar's behemoth head-on

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1259 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eurogamer

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It's got cool cars, crime, a big newly introduced city to explore, and the potential to hoover up so much player time that many developers have chosen to give it the widest berth possible.
  • Escape Academy 2: Back 2 School, a first-person puzzle adventure with a popular predecessor, was originally set to launch this September, but like many games this year saw its release date moved.
  • Escape Academy 2's original release date might have kept it away from Grand Theft Auto 6, but it would have instead faced a potential "bloodbath" of competition from the likes of Onimusha: Way of the Sword, Blood of the Dawnwalker, Control Resonant, and more.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Grand Theft Auto 6. It's got cool cars, crime, a big newly introduced city to explore, and the potential to hoover up so much player time that many developers have chosen to give it the widest berth possible. It's led to an October uncommonly packed with big-hitters, and a November - ordinarily one of gaming's biggest months - that's near-barren. But not every developer is steering clear. Despite the potential risks, a select few have looked at GTA 6 and seen not a threat but an opportunity, so what's driving these brave souls?

Escape Academy 2: Back 2 School, a first-person puzzle adventure with a popular predecessor, was originally set to launch this September, but like many games this year saw its release date moved. However, its developer bucked the industry trend, shifting its sequel not away from GTA 6's orbit, but closer. "The thing that scares me more than this monocultural event - GTA 6 - is releasing in a week when there are like 15 good games rather than one significant one", Coin Crew Games co-founder Wyatt Bushnell tells me when I ask about the studio's decision.

Escape Academy 2's original release date might have kept it away from Grand Theft Auto 6, but it would have instead faced a potential "bloodbath" of competition from the likes of Onimusha: Way of the Sword, Blood of the Dawnwalker, Control Resonant, and more. "That was our rationale," Bushnell states. "We can still cut into the GTA stuff, but it would have been a lot harder in September and October.".

In a recent development, it helps, notes Bushnell, that Escape Academy 2 and Grand Theft Auto 6 - one a contemplative puzzle game, the other a blockbuster action spectacle - are serving very different crowds. That's a sentiment echoed by David Lowey, Atari's senior director of sales and marketing. Atari has similarly bucked industry trends and is releasing two games - Godzilla Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered and Barbie Rewind - in the now largely vacant November window.

When we speak, Lowey says there's a clear logic to smaller companies "sneaking" into spots that bigger-budget games can't risk filling, especially if their games differ greatly from Grand Theft Auto 6. "Look at Barbie Rewind coming out on the 12th," he elaborates. "It's a retro game, so it'll pull in people who grew up with these games [and] there's the cosy dreamhouse design at the core ... which is a vastly different game type to GTA 6 and plenty of other games.

"It's not an FPS, not a high-octane action game, there's not a lot of combat," Lowey continues. "It's designed to be the exact opposite. It's a game you're meant to curl up in a chair and play." And while he acknowledges the "reality of modern gaming" means there'll be some audience overlap between Barbie Rewind and GTA 6 players - "These sort of older ideas of what people play by gender and age have been smashed", he says - it "won't be the biggest overlap in the world". That, then, makes going toe-to-toe an easier bet.

Sources indicate that but for Bushnell and Escape Academy, there's another consideration making GTA 6's launch window feel less of a risk: longer-tail sales. "The traditional thinking is that you have this big release and make all of your money in those first two weeks," he explains. "I don't think that holds a tonne of water anymore. The vast majority of sales for Escape Academy were made well after its release. The reality is with digital distribution, discounting, and the fact there is this shelf of games, we're in a world where games last far longer than their initial launch." That means it's less of a concern if GTA 6 sucks up everyone's attention for a few weeks.

And for Atari's David Lowey, Godzilla Destroy All Monsters and Barbie Rewind's proximity to GTA 6 has brought added benefits, enabling both games to capitalise on the hype around Rockstar's open-world epic in their own way. "One of the most rewarding things has been the fascination we've seen online around the proximity of Godzilla, Barbie, and GTA," he says.

Sources indicate that the community has found it easy to root for games releasing in the behemoth shadow of GTA 6. Godzilla Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered - an updated version of the 2002 GameCube party fighting game, which released on 3rd November - has been dubbed, tongue in cheek, the "GTA killer" by fans, while others have joked that Rockstar is "running scared" from Barbie Rewind. "There's no question that this buzz based on the closeness has created player interest," adds Lowey. "In retrospect the timing worked well for us.".

There's one game, though, that isn't just orbiting GTA 6, it's facing the triple-A juggernaut head-on. Edmund McMillen, Tyler Glaiel, and publisher Nicalis are bringing The Binding of Isaac: Repentance+ to Xbox Series X/S, PlayStation 5, and Switch 2 on 19th November, the same day GTA 6 arrives. "That was [Nicalis'] idea," McMillen laughs when we speak. "'Wouldn't it be funny if...?' I was like, whatever, that's funny ... We're done, so we've got to release this month ... It's a fun experiment.".

"There's a possibility [Repentance+'s release date] wasn't that stupid an idea," McMillen adds, "and if it was a stupid idea, it's a funny stupid idea." He also hints there's a "funny stupid" thing awaiting players who do a Repentance+ daily run on any platform during GTA 6's launch...

McMillen is, though, all too aware of the impact major releases can have on other games. "My heart states it doesn't matter, but my brain has shown me it does," he explains. "When Mewgenics came out it blew up; we went past two million sales almost right off the bat. It was such a blasting, skyrocketing thing for like three weeks. Then Slay the Spire 2 came out, and it sucked everybody out. The same players who liked Mewgenics, they were Slay The Spire players. So they all went woosh and right over ... When a latest thing comes out, people all move to the new thing ... You can see numbers go from astronomical to very small, and then if the game is good, it'll trickle back in.".

The way McMillen sees it, though, GTA 6 isn't immune to this natural ebb of flow of player interest either, and its pull might not be as long-lasting as some fear. "I know a lot of people buy Grand Theft Auto. I don't know how many people play Grand Theft Auto," he explains. "I don't know how many people are going to be sucked into this game and stay the whole time." And for McMillen, the fact GTA 6 is putting so many players in front of consoles is a positive.

In a recent development, "I think the people who like Isaac are going to play the game regardless," he says. "[But] logically, there's a record number of people who are going to be on the console the game is on at launch [because of GTA 6] ... They might be like me, play [GTA 6] for a while, and say, 'Okay, I have a console with one game, what am I going to play next?' Then, you know, a rising tide will raise all ships. I think Grand Theft Auto will bring people back to consoles, because consoles are abysmal right now. Sales are bad and no one is playing anything. People own next-gen consoles and they're just sitting there...".

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Fugaku, Japan's most powerful supercomputer and the ninth-fastest on the planet, has suffered a suspected data breach.
  • By November 14, the investigation had confirmed that unauthorized access to Fugaku had taken place, with access also blocked at that time.
  • According to recent reports, following the discovery of the breach, Riken reported the incident to Japan's Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology (MEXT).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Fugaku, Japan's most powerful supercomputer and the ninth-fastest on the planet, has suffered a suspected data breach. The news was revealed by its operator, Riken, which is the country's national research institute, with the outfit also confirming that personal information relating to more than 4,000 users of Fugaku was potentially taken during the breach. Further, the information of 375 users of Riken's Rikyu AI supercomputer was also possibly taken. The personal information includes names, email addresses, research files, and even the authentication information that was used to access the supercomputers and related services. The Japan Times reports that the operators of Fugaku first became aware of suspicious communications on November 12, with those suspicions then triggering an investigation.

By November 14, the investigation had confirmed that unauthorized access to Fugaku had taken place, with access also blocked at that time. The investigation identified that hackers had used the supercomputer's externally accessible operational status dashboard as the springboard for the hack between November 10 and November 13. Now taken offline while security concerns are addressed, the dashboard allowed the hackers to gain access to the system's internal network, but beyond that, details are scarce. Riken does not yet know — or at least, it isn't saying — the full story of how the hackers gained access to Fugaku as a whole. But it has confirmed that some servers had unauthorized software installed.

According to recent reports, following the discovery of the breach, Riken reported the incident to Japan's Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology (MEXT). Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara has since confirmed that MEXT and Riken were working together to investigate what happened and ascertain the full scope of the breach itself. “Fugaku plays a vital role in our country’s research and development infrastructure, so it is key that they prioritize security while limiting the impact on research activities,” Kihara is reported to have said.

Located at Riken’s Center for Computational Science in Kobe, Fugaku officially came online in March of 2021 after being developed in collaboration with Fujitsu for a cost of around ¥130 billion (approximately $817 million in 2026). It became the world's fastest supercomputer before being overtaken by Frontier, an exascale supercomputer housed at the Department of Energy's Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility (OLCF) in Tennessee.

It has been revealed that the fastest supercomputer right now in operation is China's LineShine. It recently retained its crown as the fastest on the planet amid a move away from traditional supercomputers to AI data centers.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A latest law from the European Union could impact the way ads from influencers and pay-to-win items in games work, especially those that target minors.
  • Industry observers note that back on November 10, the European Union laid out its first proposal for what they’re calling the Digital Fairness Act.
  • The European Union highlighted things such as “manipulative marketing tactics or hidden fees” as targets of the bill, but they’re also looking at advertisements from influencers too.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A latest law from the European Union could impact the way ads from influencers and pay-to-win items in games work, especially those that target minors.

Industry observers note that back on November 10, the European Union laid out its first proposal for what they’re calling the Digital Fairness Act. In short, the DFA is looking to clamp down on “unfair commercial practices” that are regularly seen online.

The European Union highlighted things such as “manipulative marketing tactics or hidden fees” as targets of the bill, but they’re also looking at advertisements from influencers too.

While influencers are right now required to use hashtags like ad, sponsored, and gifted on their content, the Digital Fairness Act wants to strengthen that. “Clear disclosure of influencer marketing, requiring influencers to be transparent about commercial content and preventing the exploitation of the trust of minors in their audience,” the EU pointed out as one of the “key” parts of the proposal.

Additionally, pay-to-win and pay-to-progress items in games have also been highlighted as part of the fresh act.

In a recent development, “Fairness by design, with the option for consumers to turn off addictive design features that encourage excessive or compulsive spending, such as persistent prompts. The proposal will also restrict unfair practices that encourage overspending, for example by banning gambling-like features for minors, such as pay-to-win and pay-to-progress,” they added.

It’s unclear as to how broad that anti-pay-to-win protection would be, seeing as there are continual arguments about what can be classified as P2W.

EU intends sweeping social media and AI chatbot restrictions for kids under 15.

European Union makes legislative change that will change in-game purchases forever.

New Microsoft patent could put in-game ads after boss fights, multiplayer matches and cutscenes.

Games like Call of Duty and Fortnite note that items are not sold as granting a competitive advantage, but players have found ways to get a leg-up with weapons and character skins.

There would also be a crackdown on “fake claims” that tell people to rush to buy items due to apparent low stock and changing prices.

In the United States, a number of ticket resale websites have sued the District of Columbia over a upcoming law that will cap the resale price of tickets at 10% above face value.

It has been revealed that weekly. Free. One click to leave.

According to recent reports, 7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

Picking an ecommerce platform is really a decision about which layers you want to own: the storefront, the catalog and order logic, the payment flow, and the hosting underneath. Every platform below draws that line in a different place. If you have already settled the front-end question with a comparison like SitePoint's Astro vs Next.js guide, the next question is what sits behind it. Prices are from each vendor's pricing page as of November 2026.

Shopify is the fully managed option. Basic costs $29 a month with card rates from 2.9% plus 30 cents, and a 2% fee applies to orders processed through a third-party gateway on that proposal. Developers get two routes: Liquid themes, or Hydrogen, Shopify's headless toolkit, where your framework owns routing and rendering and Hydrogen supplies the Storefront API client and cart. Templates exist for React Router on Oxygen and for Next.js on Vercel. Plus starts at $2,300 a month.

It has been revealed that whop is a business platform for taking payments and sending payouts, and it sits under a storefront you have already built rather than replacing it. The Checkout element runs in the browser with no server code and no API key on the page. You pass your own order ID as metadata, Whop copies it onto the payment, and your server fulfills from a signed webhook that follows the Standard Webhooks spec. Domestic cards cost 2.7% plus 30 cents with no monthly fee, buyers see payment methods chosen by their location across 195 countries, and the same balance pays out in over 200 countries, including to affiliates or sellers you onboard. Whop's own guide shows how to integrate a checkout API into a Next.js storefront end to end. The trade-off is that there is no catalog or shipping engine; you collect address fields at checkout and trigger fulfillment from the webhook.

WooCommerce is a free plugin on WordPress you host yourself, so you own updates, security, and performance. Its payment gateway, WooPayments, charges US merchants 2.9% plus 30 cents per card transaction, 1.5% more for international cards, 2% for currency conversion, and $25 per dispute. Everything is PHP hooks and filters, which makes it the natural pick for agencies already living in WordPress and the wrong pick for anyone who does not want to run a server.

It has been revealed that bigCommerce hosts the back end and lets you bring any front end. Core is $29 a month billed annually, capped at $30,000 in trailing annual sales, and intends auto-upgrade as volume grows. There are no platform fees when you use an embedded payment provider, and a 2% fee on Core if you use another one. Catalyst, its reference storefront, is built on Next.js, React Server Components, and the Storefront GraphQL API, and deploys to Vercel.

Medusa is an open-source commerce framework in Node.js and TypeScript, with an MIT-licensed core and a commercial enterprise edition. SitePoint covered it when it was still a young Shopify alternative; it now has over 37,000 GitHub stars. Self-hosting is free. Medusa Cloud starts at $29 a month for development, $99 for launch, and $299 for scale, with no percentage of sales, and the company indicates you can export your data and self-host at any point.

Recent findings suggest that saleor is a GraphQL-native, API-only commerce platform written in Python and released under the BSD-3 license. Self-hosting is free. Saleor Cloud starts at $1,599 a month for up to $200,000 in monthly sales, with 0.8% on orders above that, and $3,999 a month at the next tier. It is built for teams with a dedicated engineering function and a large catalog, which is exactly who should pay that price.

Sources indicate that own only the storefront, and Shopify or BigCommerce will carry the rest. Own everything, and Medusa or Saleor give you a back end you can read. Already on WordPress, and WooCommerce is the obvious fit. Already have a storefront in Next.js or Astro and only need the money to move, and Whop is the shortest path. Whichever you pick, the checkout is where disputes start, so log what SitePoint's friendly fraud guide for developers recommends from day one.

Umamusume fans in the US can now order food inspired by Special Week, Oguri Cap, and Haru Urara, alongside a slew of collectible merch.

The collaboration is with Japanese ramen restaurant Tsujita, which will be offering themed meals across its locations in Los Angeles, New Jersey, and Houston until December 20.

During the horse girl-themed food collab, customers can order five menu items inspired by Umamusume characters, including spicy miso ramen based on Special Week and a massive Oguri Cap rice bowl that reveals fried chicken when flipped upside down.

Kicking things off is Special Week’s Golden Spicy Cheese Miso Ramen, which is available until November 30 and takes inspiration from her Hokkaido roots. The bowl comes filled with grilled corn, melted cheese, bean sprouts, and a carrot-shaped garnish (can’t forget the carrots).

Next up is Fine Motion’s Cajun seafood tsukemen, a dipping noodle dish that pairs rich seafood broth with a spicy Cajun kick. The broth has shrimp, mussels, corn, sausage, bell peppers, and lime in it. So it’s a good pick if you’re a fan of rich seafood flavours. Fine Motion’s dish will be available from December 1 through December 20.

Industry observers note that just like in the anime, Oguri Cap’s Upside-Down Fried Chicken Bowl arrives as a massive mound of rice. You’ll need to flip the bowl to reveal chunks of fried chicken and egg, while Rice Shower’s Purple Bun Set pairs pork chashu and fried chicken with purple cabbage coleslaw.

And in typical last-place fashion, Haru Urara gets a Cheerful Carrot & Strawberry Float that combines generous helpings of carrot, mango, and strawberry, topped with a carrot ribbon. Not a bad call if you’re looking for something bright and fruity to wash all that ramen down with.

Umamusume x KFC collab includes carrot dip and more anime-inspired menu items.

Each Uma-themed menu order also comes with one of four randomly distributed coasters, which feature chibi versions of the horse girls. Fans can also buy a $35 T-shirt or a $10 blind bag containing a random pin and sticker.

The collaboration is available at Tsujita’s Arts District location in Los Angeles, Fort Lee in Fresh Jersey, and Houston in Texas until December 20.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A restaurant in North Carolina has hit out at “miserable and entitled” customers after their rules about tipping went viral on social media, and people thought that the answer would be to review bomb them.

Tipping in restaurants and bar has long been a divisive topic, with different places handling it in their own unique ways. Some establishments put an automatic gratuity charge on bills, while others still leave it up to the customer.

On November 15, the Freeman’s Grub & Pub in Greensboro, North Carolina, come under fire on the EndTipping subreddit after one user flagged a notice about their tipping rules.

“If our employees have two separate instances of you not tipping well without explanation, we will add a 20% autograt fee on your bill,” the rules state. “Your receipts will be saved if this is the case, and you are welcome to question it,” they also noted, urging customers to leave a name and number if they have any complaints.

The restaurant’s co-owner, Kevin Purcell, responded to the backlash on November 16, noting that he had been hit with review bombs online.

Industry observers note that “It is 2026, and you should know by now the rules of engagement and expectations to tip at a bar or restaurant. Our staff is beyond competent; they’re professionals at what they do. You’re expected to tip for the great to excellent service that they provide,” Purcell noted.

“Servers everywhere talk s*it when you leave about how pathetic it is that you still don’t know the very basic rules of dining out at this point in your miserable and entitled existence.”.

Restaurant blasts customers for “stealing” over viral dine-and-dash videos.

Customer removes 15% automatic tip after server refuses to give him tap water.

Customer removes automatic 18% tip added to their bill and people are furious.

Purcell added that if there are genuine mistakes, then the restaurants does assist on that front, but they “take pride in providing a top-tier dining experience.”.

He noted that the restaurant will “stand behind our controversial policy and amazing staff,” despite what may come.

Industry observers note that the response has garnered plenty of sympathy and fightback from customers who want to support the restaurant too. “I have never been to your restaurant but will go soon,” one said.

Sources indicate that “Just left a review! You guys are the best, it’s great seeing restaurant owners truly care about their staff” another commented. “Thank you for being an exemplary business,” another added.

How we test enterprise SSDs

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3223 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that after a hiatus of several years, Tom's Hardware is expanding its in-depth testing and analysis to enterprise and data center SSDs.
  • Recent findings suggest that comprehensive reviews of enterprise and data center SSDs are therefore more vital than ever.
  • Reviewing enterprise and data center SSDs required us to build a workstation that could truly challenge these drives.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that after a hiatus of several years, Tom's Hardware is expanding its in-depth testing and analysis to enterprise and data center SSDs. Consumer SSDs and conventional hard drives lack the performance and endurance for extensive AI workloads. This has increased demand for enterprise SSDs. Form factors like U.2, U.3, E3.S, and E1.S, once rare, are now common in high-end workstations and home labs. These enterprise storage solutions provide higher capacities, better performance, and greater reliability than consumer drives.

Recent findings suggest that comprehensive reviews of enterprise and data center SSDs are therefore more vital than ever. Buying a drive of this caliber is a major decision and a significant investment for organizations of all sizes. With this latest venture, Tom's Hardware will continue to help buyers make informed decisions with comprehensive reviews and performance analyses.

Reviewing enterprise and data center SSDs required us to build a workstation that could truly challenge these drives. This project would not have been possible without the support of several component makers, including Asus, Corsair, G.Skill, Icy Dock, and Noctua, who made the workstation a reality, a challenging prospect in the current market.

The Xeon 658X, a 24-core, 48-thread chip from the Granite Rapids family with a 4.9 GHz boost clock speed, powers the testing workstation. Single-core performance and total core count matter just as much when reviewing storage. Clock speed determines how many IOPS one core can push and how fast it answers a single request, while 24 cores let us spread a drive's load across eight fio jobs and later test several drives at once. The Xeon 658X ticks all those boxes.

In a recent development, we've entrusted the Xeon 658X's cooling to Noctua's NH-U14S DX-4677 air cooler, which supports both LGA4677 and LGA4710 sockets. The single-tower CPU air cooler delivers high-performance cooling at very low noise levels thanks to its dual NF-A15 140mm cooling fans.

Industry observers note that with its server-grade components and robust enterprise features, the Asus Pro WS W890E-Sage SE is the ideal motherboard to pair with the Xeon 658X. Its extensive feature set includes an onboard MCIO x8 connection, split into x4/x4, that allows for evaluating two U.2 or U.3 drives. The board also provides seven PCIe 5.0 expansion slots (six at x16 and one at x8) to fully leverage the Xeon 658X’s 128 PCIe 5.0 lanes, so the SSDs and graphics cards never hit bandwidth limits.

We're still in need of support for an RTX Pro graphics card, which would be an invaluable asset for enterprise SSD reviews for real-world AI workloads, but our current test platform allows us to test the most crucial aspects of performance.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Despite the memory and storage shortage, G.Skill and Corsair have stepped up to provide crucial components for our enterprise SSD test bench. G.Skill sent a G5 DDR5-6400 C32 64GB (4x16GB) R-DIMM memory kit, which runs at the stock DDR5-5600 speed. The decision to keep it at the JEDEC baseline has nothing to do with the memory kit: Memory frequency does not affect performance in enterprise SSD tests.

Meanwhile, Corsair provided the speedy MP700 Pro XT 2TB, one of the best SSDs, as the test bench's primary storage. The PCIe 5.0 drive delivers sequential read and write speeds up to 14,900 MB/s and 14,500 MB/s, respectively, and keeps the workstation snappy, especially when it hammers enterprise drives all day long.

No power supply is better suited to the job than the Corsair HX1500i. It offers a massive 1,500W capacity with plenty of headroom for future upgrades, and it runs quietly and stably, two qualities that matter when you keep the test system running for countless hours. It is an 80 Plus Platinum power supply with at least 89% efficiency at full load.

Recent findings suggest that testing enterprise drives in a standard PCIe expansion slot is more convenient. For that purpose, Icy Dock has provided us with the ExpressSlot Elite MB221E5P-B and MB303E5P-B to accept one and two E1.S SSDs. Unlike other generic designs on the market, these adapters feature tool-less installation mechanisms that don't require removing them from the PCIe expansion slot, and they include 50mm fans for active cooling.

The list also included the ToughArmor MB218E5P-B, a 5.25-inch drive bay that supports up to eight E1.S SSDs for future projects exploring RAID arrays. To test E3.S drives, we use a JMT ADT-R27C adapter strapped to a Noctua NF-F12 industrialPPC-24V-3000 IP67 PWM cooling fan, which can run at 12V and still provide substantial airflow to actively cool the SSDs under evaluation.

According to recent reports, A TGDGamer E-ATX test bench houses the hardware for the enterprise SSD system. It may not look flashy, but it does the job, and that is what matters. As an open-air test bench, it is easy to install and remove hardware, and it eliminates variables when it comes to heat generation and buildup. The test bench also supports motherboard form factors up to SSI-EEB, so the Asus Pro WS W890E-Sage SE feels right at home.

It has been revealed that A spec sheet only tells you what a drive can do on its best day. The real world is not as pretty. The drive is mostly full, garbage collection is constantly at work, and multiple workloads are hitting it simultaneously. Our enterprise benchmark suite is built to measure the drive in service: at steady state, under load, through write bursts, and with other jobs running. Every drive gets the same automated run on the same test bench. Every result is stored with the exact parameters that produced it, so we can trace how we got there.

This can take some time. A full run takes most of a day on a 7.68TB PCIe 5.0 drive, and it writes the drive end-to-end many times over. To make life a bit easier on us, the benchmark can be run unattended, and it’s crash-resumable from the last stage. A shorter express mode handles bench checks and quick triage. When a result looks odd, express runs and variant runs, which repeat just the tests in question or change one setting, help us find the cause before we take it to the vendor.

We run the bench on a custom Debian 13 image that we build and maintain ourselves, with the suite copied in at build time. This image gets installed on the bench’s OS drive, and the kernel is pinned so every drive has the same software stack. Right now that’s Linux 7.2.6 from Debian backports, because Debian 13’s stock 6.12 kernel predates support for the Asus Pro WS W890E-Sage SE’s Intel E610 10GbE controller. The suite is also designed to be run remotely if needed, but we need a tester at the bench to switch the drives, of course.

In a recent development, debian is our pick over Ubuntu for a few reasons: it has fewer background services, no Snap, and no unattended upgrades by default. We hold the kernel so nothing changes between runs. We remove AppArmor and turn off scheduled jobs that could fire mid-run, like the weekly TRIM timer and the drive-health service that polls every drive, and the suite records any that are still running. The suite also turns off NVMe autonomous power-state transitions (APST) at the start of every run and checks that the drive reports it off, so no drive drops into a low-power state during an idle gap and adds wake-up latency to the next I/O.

Every test runs in fio 3.42, using io_uring and direct I/O against the raw block device. This means no filesystem and no page cache sitting between fio and the drive; the bench’s 64GB of RAM never caches a byte of test data. We compile fio from source because Debian’s packaged version lacks SPRandom, which we’ll get to in short order.

According to recent reports, some enterprise storage reviews run application profiles in Oracle’s Vdbench, but we decided to go full fio. This makes for a more consistent suite with one set of latency accounting across every chart. And fio is open source and actively maintained, while Vdbench hasn’t had a new release since 2018. Vdbench profiles are built from the same parts fio uses, such as read/write ratio, block-size mix, and random or sequential access, and our mixed-workload sweeps cover the common read/write ratios at 4K and 8K, though not mixed-block-size profiles. Running Vdbench ourselves wouldn’t make our results comparable to other outlets’ anyway, since they use different hardware, preconditioning, and profile definitions.

In a recent development, A key element of benchmarking SSDs is making sure the test drive is at steady state, with the performance it can sustain rather than the peak you can see after a fresh erase. Our first stage is a secure erase using nvme format. If a drive refuses, the suite falls back to a plain format, then a full-drive discard, and records which one it used.

It has been revealed that next comes preconditioning. SPRandom, SanDisk’s open-source contribution to fio, is a faster alternative to filling the drive over and over for hours. It takes user capacity and over-provisioning (OP) as inputs, which SanDisk states lets it reach a steady-state layout in just one pass. Overprovisioning (OP) is inferred from the capacity point or given by the tester. NVMe drives don’t report their raw flash, so a 7.68TB drive like our first one, assumed to sit on 8TiB of actual NAND, works out to having about 14.5% OP.

We don’t take SPRandom’s result on faith. A steady-state gate follows, running 4K random writes at queue depth 256 (QD256) until the drive’s write speed stops moving. It uses the two tests from the Storage Networking Industry Association’s (SNIA) steady-state rule, with limits ten times tighter, applied to the last 30 minutes: split into five six-minute rounds, the round averages must sit within 2% of one another, and the trend line across the window can’t move more than 1%.

Industry observers note that that takes a while, but that’s the point: an earlier, looser version of the gate passed our first drive while its write speed was still climbing. The whole settling curve is saved with every run, and a drive that doesn’t settle within three hours is marked as not reaching steady state, though the run continues. As a backstop, the suite repeats the four-corner 4K write after the random sweep, hours later, and flags the run if the two results differ by more than 3%.

The suite also checks its own results as it goes. If a test’s slowest moment falls below 70% of its average, that test is run again on the spot. If a point in the random sweep lands more than 10% off the curve set by its neighbors, it’s measured again before the drive is erased for the sequential tests. Both results are kept, and any re-test is noted in the review.

Following the random tests, the tool erases the drive again and writes it end to end once, with 128K sequential writes at QD64. We run it before the sequential and AI tests, so the drive is conditioned with the kind of I/O we’re about to measure. It matters because sequential writes can swing wildly on a randomly written drive: on our first test drive, the fastest result was more than three times the slowest. After a sequential fill, they held flat from QD2 through QD1024, at both 128K and 1MB.

Industry observers note that drives are formatted to 512-byte logical blocks when they support it, so our block size sweep can go down to 512-byte transfers, which a 4K-native namespace can’t issue. SNIA’s enterprise IOPS test uses 512-byte transfers too, and Kioxia pitches 512-byte access for its GP Series, which is aimed at GPU-initiated storage. Drives without a 512-byte format are tested as shipped, and their sub-4K results are marked unsupported. The switch happens in the same format command as the secure erase, so it adds no time.

In a recent development, A fast enough SSD will happily benchmark your host, or your tools, instead, and our early runs turned up three ways that could happen. The first is CPU idle states, or C-states: waking our Xeon 658X cores from their deepest idle state can take up to 170 microseconds, and at QD1 that directly impacts the results. Holding the cores awake for the whole run cut the first drive’s average 4K QD1 read latency by about a sixth.

The second is the CPU itself: a single fio job can saturate its core well short of what a PCIe 5.0 drive can manage. Split across eight jobs, the same test runs several times faster, so random tests now spread their queue depth across up to eight fio jobs. That’s also why fast cores, and enough of them, matter for this test bench.

The third is fio itself. By default, fio seeds its random generator the same way every run, so it replays the same sequence of random offsets, and each random write test rewrites the previous test’s blocks in the same order. On our first drive, that was the main reason 4K random writes came in at more than twice the sustained figure. Every random test now runs with a fresh random seed.

It has been revealed that what we don’t change matters, too. Completions arrive by interrupt rather than polling, and the IOMMU stays in its default mode, because that’s how most applications use a drive. On our first drive, polling and IOMMU passthrough would each have shaved some latency off 4K QD1 writes.

Interrupts also set a ceiling at the other end of the scale: this bench tops out near 2.8 million 4K random read IOPS, and adding fio jobs doesn’t lift it, though polling does. So on the fastest drives, our 4K random read result can sit below the spec sheet’s, and that’s our bench’s limit, not the drive’s. Our low queue depth latencies, writes especially, run higher than a tuned host would show, but they’re closer to what you’d actually see. To show the drive’s limit at both ends, the suite repeats three tests with polled I/O at the end of the random stage: the 4K random read peak, plus 4K random reads and writes at QD1. Those results get their own charts and never mix into the main ones.

4K random read and write at QD256; 128K and 1MB sequential read and write at QD64.

The headline numbers, measured on a preconditioned drive instead of fresh out of the box.

4K and 8K, QD1 to QD4096, eight read/write mixes from 100% read to 100% write.

Servers rarely run flat out; QD1 is what latency-bound software feels, and 8K is a common database page size.

4K random read at QD1024 across eight jobs, plus 4K random read and write at QD1, all with polled I/O.

What the drive can do with the host’s interrupt overhead out of the way; the results to set against a spec sheet.

128K and 1MB sequential reads and writes, QD1 to QD1024.

How much parallelism a drive needs to reach full speed; low queue depths are what a single restore or scan gets.

Random reads and writes from 512 bytes to 1MB at QD32.

Writes smaller than a drive’s mapping unit can pay a read-modify-write penalty; large blocks show its bandwidth cap.

4K and 8K reads and writes at QD1, QD4, and QD16, from the median (P50) to the 99.999th percentile (P99.999).

Averages hide the stalls applications notice; at a million IOPS, the slowest 0.001% is still ten requests a second.

4K 70/30 at 13 queue depths from QD1 to QD4096, plotted as a share of the drive’s own peak.

Finds the load where latency starts to climb.

One hour of 4K random writes at QD256.

Whether sustained writes hold a flat line or sawtooth as garbage collection struggles.

4K QD1 reads for four minutes right after a heavy write burst.

How far reads drop after heavy writes, and how fast they recover.

Write bursts after idle gaps of 0 to 300 seconds.

How much write speed a quiet spell buys back.

Database I/O patterns (simulated).

4K QD1 log writes with a sync after each, a random 8K 70/30 mix at QD16, and a 256K sequential read scan.

Log-write latency, page I/O, and analytics scans, without benchmarking a database’s RAM cache.

Checkpoint-sized saves and restores modeled on 8B- and 70B-class models (105GiB over eight writers, 912GiB over 64).

Time until the slowest writer finishes, which is when a real checkpoint would be done.

A fixed 4K read load, alone and during a checkpoint save.

What a checkpoint does to serving traffic on the same drive.

Drive temperature through the hour-long sustained write test.

Measured against the drive’s own warning and critical thresholds.

In a recent development, some things are out of scope by design. We review drives; we don’t certify them. That rules out dual-port failover, power-loss validation, and single-root I/O virtualization (SR-IOV), which belong in a qualification lab. We’ll add tests when they prove themselves on the bench. Many of the tests in the table are old standbys and still earn their place. Others are newer and require further explanation.

Sources indicate that for one, we chart latency against load: the 70/30 4K mix from the random sweep, at 13 queue depths from QD1 to QD4096, with throughput shown as a share of the drive’s own peak. Tail latency climbs as the load grows, and the point where it turns sharply upward (on our first drive, that was write latency) represents the practical operating ceiling, or the load you can initiative a server around without giving up low latency.

We also test write-to-read recovery, which measures how a drive’s reads hold up after a heavy write burst. A few minutes of 4K random writes at QD256 leave the drive with cleanup to do, and QD1 reads are then timed over the next four minutes. If a drive is still busy collecting garbage, it will read slower before climbing back; the extent and duration of the drop are the result.

According to recent reports, idle recovery measures what downtime buys back. After a minute of sustained writes, the drive sits idle for anywhere from zero to five minutes, then a 10-second write burst, logged second by second, shows whether background cleanup freed enough blocks to run faster.

Checkpoint interference shows what an AI checkpoint does to anything else sharing the drive. A light 4K read load, which stands in for inference or database queries, runs alone, and then again during a checkpoint save. Each read is timed from when it was due, not when it was sent, so reads stuck waiting behind a stalled one count too.

It has been revealed that lastly, we test thermals. Drive temperature is tracked through the hour-long sustained write test and charted against the drive's own warning and critical thresholds.

In a recent development, the full process means every drive is treated the same and compared fairly, with a method built to give the same results run after run. This allows us to provide a level playing field built on accurate and repeatable performance characterization.

Shane Downing is a Contributing Writer for Tom’s Hardware, covering consumer storage, PC hardware, and AI.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Five years ago, players exploring GTA Trilogy: The Definitive Edition noticed something unusual inside the Lil’ Probe’Inn, a UFO-themed bar in San Andreas.
  • It has been revealed that among the photographs on the wall was a picture of a suburban house with palm trees and a UFO flying overhead.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A mysterious GTA 6 screenshot discovered in San Andreas Definitive Edition back in 2021 has finally been found in Rockstar’s new game, confirming a theory that predates even the infamous 2022 hack.

Five years ago, players exploring GTA Trilogy: The Definitive Edition noticed something unusual inside the Lil’ Probe’Inn, a UFO-themed bar in San Andreas.

It has been revealed that among the photographs on the wall was a picture of a suburban house with palm trees and a UFO flying overhead. Unlike the other images, which came from existing Rockstar titles, nobody could identify where it was from.

Dexerto reported on the discovery in November 2021, with fans theorizing that Rockstar had secretly included the first-ever GTA 6 screenshot.

Now, with GTA 6 finally here, it turns out they were right.

The same day the game was released in Upcoming Zealand, a player named Jared from the GTA 6 mapping community discovered the house in Belville, located in Leonida’s Leonard County.

The building is almost identical to its 2021 appearance, right down to the garage, palm trees, and surrounding vegetation.

According to recent reports, all credit goes to Jared from the GTA VI Mapping server.The house is located in Belville. (https://t.co/hWt1Koz3uz) pic.twitter.com/t2ZsSRPQFI.

However, players who break into the garage will discover something even more bizarre.

Inside is the hideout of a conspiracy theorist who has seemingly figured out that he’s living inside a video game.

In a recent development, notes scattered around the garage reveal that the resident has been trying to escape Leonida, but can’t purchase a plane ticket to Los Santos or drive beyond the state’s borders. He’s even considering fleeing by boat.

The conspiracy theorist has also noticed NPCs who look identical, neighbors unable to enter their own homes, people glitching through walls, and buildings with nothing behind their locked doors.

GTA Trilogy players think they solved the ‘GTA 6’ house screenshot mystery.

First GTA 6 screenshot? GTA Trilogy players make big discovery in San Andreas.

GTA Online insider states “leaked” GTA 6 screenshot mystery will finally be solved soon.

There’s even a graph showing an enormous spike in violent crime alongside numerous references to the number six.

Recent findings suggest that the photo Rockstar added to GTA San Andreas Definitive Edition in 2021 was a real GTA 6 photo.You can visit that house to find more conspiracy theories hidden inside. pic.twitter.com/5vxNFBmsSQ.

In a recent development, perhaps most interestingly, the resident identifies two individuals, known only as J and L, who appear immune to the strange limitations of his world. These are seemingly references to GTA 6 protagonists Jason and Lucia.

We’ll have to see if there’s even more to this discovery as players continue to explore Leonida and see everything the world has to offer.

The find is especially remarkable because the original screenshot surfaced in November 2021, nearly a year before the massive September 2022 Rockstar hack exposed early GTA 6 gameplay.

It’s unclear whether Rockstar planned the garage’s fourth-wall-breaking Easter egg all those years ago or added it after seeing the community obsess over the house.

Either way, the developer managed to hide a glimpse of GTA 6 in plain sight years before its official reveal.

#46812. What is Model Routing in AI?

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1938 w)

What is Model Routing in AI?

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1938 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sitepoint

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
  • "Do you know the closest ATM?" and "I was charged twice, the refund never arrived, and now my card is blocked" are both customer messages.
  • A router looks at each request and sends it to the cheapest model that can handle it, and keeps the expensive model for the requests that need it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Weekly. Free. One click to leave.

7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

"Do you know the closest ATM?" and "I was charged twice, the refund never arrived, and now my card is blocked" are both customer messages. Most AI apps send both to the same large model and pay large-model prices for each one.

Model routing fixes that. A router looks at each request and sends it to the cheapest model that can handle it, and keeps the expensive model for the requests that need it.

In this guide we'll cover what model routing is, how routers decide, and what it saves. Then we'll build a small router in about 60 lines of JavaScript and run it over 200 customer messages. At one setting it matched a large model's accuracy for about a third of the cost. At another it came within a point and a half for 89% less.

Model routing in AI is the practice of sending each request to the model best suited to it, instead of sending every request to one model. A router sits between your app and a pool of models, reads each request, and picks a model based on what you care about: cost, speed, or quality.

You'll also see it called AI model routing, LLM routing, or LLM model routing. They all mean the same thing. The pool might be a small and a large model from one provider, or models from several providers behind one API.

Sources indicate that the idea rests on one observation: most requests are easy. A small model answers them as well as a large one, in a fraction of the time and for a fraction of the price. The router's whole job is finding the hard ones.

The diagram below demonstrates a typical AI model routing architecture.

Model routing works in three steps: the router reads the request, decides which model should answer it, and forwards the request to that model. The middle step is where routers differ. Routing tools decide which model to use in one of four ways.

According to recent reports, rule-based routing uses rules you write by hand. Requests from free-plan users go to a small model. Anything tagged as code goes to a coding model. Prompts over a certain length go to a model with a bigger context window. It's simple, predictable, and free to run, but the rules only know what you thought of in advance.

Intelligent model routing uses a model to make the decision. A small, fast classifier reads each request and predicts which model in the pool will answer it well. You'll also see it called smart or dynamic model routing.

Sources indicate that two more terms come up here. Task-aware routing picks a model by the kind of job, like summarising, coding, or answering a support question. Context-aware routing also looks at what surrounds the request, like the conversation so far, the user, or the tools available.

In a recent development, the big platforms work this way. Microsoft describes its Foundry model router as "a trained language model" that picks a model for each prompt in real time. Google states Gemini Notebook uses its upcoming Decisions API as a real-time router, serving everyday queries with up to 40% lower latency. I've tested the Google Decisions API against Jev on the same messages we'll use below.

Industry observers note that cascade routing tries the cheapest model first and only moves up when the answer isn't good enough. The usual test is confidence: if the cheap model is sure, keep its answer. If it isn't, send the request to a stronger model. It's also called confidence-based routing, and it's what we'll build below.

Sources indicate that A cascade needs no separate classifier, because the first model's own confidence does the routing. The trade-off is that escalated requests pay for two models and wait for both.

Industry observers note that fallback routing is about staying up, not saving money. If a model times out, hits a rate limit, or its provider has an outage, the router sends the request to the next model on a list. Most production routers combine fallbacks with one of the three methods above.

The main benefits of model routing in AI systems are lower cost, faster responses, and fewer outages, without giving up quality on the hard requests.

We'll build a cascade router for a job every support tool has: sorting customer messages. Each message gets one of ten labels, like atm support or request refund.

The test set is 200 messages from Banking77, a public set of banking support messages: ten labels, 20 messages each. They're the same 200 messages from my zero shot classification test, which is where the single-model numbers below come from.

Put both keys in a .env file and run the examples with node --env-file=.env. It's the same setup as in my guide to getting a YouTube API key.

Sources indicate that create router.mjs. The first function sends the message to Jev with one multiple-choice question, and returns the label Jev picked along with its confidence:.

Confidence runs from 0 to 1. When nearly all the probability sits on one label, it's close to 1. When Jev is torn between two labels, it drops.

In a recent development, the second function asks Claude Opus 5.5 the same question. The output_config block limits the answer to one of our labels, so there's no free text to parse. SitePoint's guide to LLM structured output with JSON Schema explains how that works.

The router itself is about a dozen lines:.

If Jev is at least 80% confident, its answer goes straight back. If not, Claude answers instead. And if Claude fails, the router falls back to Jev's answer, because a shaky answer beats an error page.

Try it on an easy message and a harder one:.

Jev was sure about the lost card. On the ATM question it leaned towards card acceptance with a confidence of 0.64, so the router asked Claude, which got it right.

Because cheap, strong, and threshold are options, the same function routes between any two models.

Sources indicate that model routing reduces AI costs by keeping easy requests on a cheap model and paying for the expensive one only when it's needed. Here's what that looked like on our 200 messages, starting with each model on its own:.

Opus gets six more messages right out of 200, and costs more than 120 times as much.

Now the router, at four confidence thresholds:.

Recent findings suggest that speed improved too. At the 0.8 threshold, the messages Jev kept came back in a median of 227 ms. The ones that escalated took about 2.1 seconds, because they waited for both models.

A note on method: I ran every message through both models once and saved the answers, then replayed the router over them at each threshold. That's how you compare thresholds without paying for the same test four times.

Recent findings suggest that then I ran the router live to check. At 0.95 it scored the same 95.0% and sent 61 messages to Opus. At 0.8 it scored 93.5% and sent 20, a point under the replay. Two answers moved: one of Jev's confidence scores landed at 0.82 instead of 0.78, just over the line, and Opus changed its answer on one message. Scores near the threshold shift a little between runs, so leave yourself a margin.

Industry observers note that the choice of cheap model matters less than you'd think. With Google's Gemini Decision 1 in first place instead of Jev, a 0.7 threshold reached the same 95% for US$0.28 per 1,000 messages.

Model routing can cost a little quality, and the threshold decides how much. In our test the gap to Opus ranged from nothing at 0.95 to two points at 0.7.

The loss comes from one place: answers the cheap model got wrong while feeling sure. At the 0.8 threshold, Jev kept five wrong answers because its confidence was above the line. Opus got four of those five wrong as well, so only one was a real loss: "Do all ATMs take this card?", which Jev filed under card acceptance with a confidence of 0.91.

Escalating isn't risk-free either. On one message, Jev had the right label with a confidence of 0.44, and Opus overruled it with the wrong one.

To optimize costs using AI model routing, measure first, route second, and keep measuring. These six steps cover LLM model routing cost optimization for any pair of models:.

Recent findings suggest that the return is easy to estimate once you know the split. If nine in ten requests stay on a model that costs 1% as much, the bill drops by about 89%, which is what we measured.

Several inference providers have multi-model routing built in, and most AI gateway platforms support model routing too, so you don't have to write your own. As of November 2026, these are the top model routing solutions for AI apps. Each name links to the tool's model routing docs:.

It has been revealed that hosted model routing platforms for large language models decide for you, which is the fastest way to start. A hand-built router like ours takes more work, but you choose the signal and you can see why every request went where it did.

An LLM router is the component that does model routing for large language models. It can be a function in your own code, like the one in this guide, a hosted model such as Microsoft Foundry's model router, or a feature of an AI gateway.

Smart model routing is another name for intelligent model routing: a model, not a hand-written rule, decides where each request goes. Dynamic model routing means the same thing.

According to recent reports, the ROI of AI model routing depends on how much of your traffic a cheaper model can handle. In our test, a 0.8 threshold kept 89.5% of messages on the cheap model and cut the cost per 1,000 messages from US$1.96 to US$0.22, for about a point of accuracy. The build was about 60 lines of code.

OpenRouter's auto model routing works through its Auto Router. You set the model to openrouter/auto, and a decision model picks a model and a reasoning effort for each request. You pay the standard rate of whichever model it selects, with no extra fee.

According to recent reports, openClaw model routing is a primary model plus an ordered list of fallbacks. In the OpenClaw model routing configuration you set agents.defaults.model.primary and agents.defaults.model.fallbacks, and an agent can override the fallback list. When a model fails, OpenClaw first rotates auth profiles on the same provider, then moves to the next model on the list, as its model failover docs describe. That makes it fallback routing, not cost-based routing.

An AI gateway simplifies model routing by putting every model behind one API, one set of keys, and one place for logs. Your app calls the gateway, and the routing rules live in config instead of code, so changing a model doesn't need a deploy.

Mid-stream failover is when a router switches models after a streamed response has already started, because the first model failed partway through. It's the hardest kind of failover, because the user has already seen part of an answer. Many routers only fail over before the first token arrives and return an error after that, so check what your gateway does.
