📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Phison’s Pascari X201P meets its rated specs and pairs 12 GB/s sequential writes with a steady 600K random write IOPS, making short work of AI checkpoints.
  • It has been revealed that why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you.
  • Phison is serious about enterprise storage, and the Pascari X201P was not released lightly; it came in the night, under NDA, alongside this week’s Supercomputing 2026 event.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Phison’s Pascari X201P meets its rated specs and pairs 12 GB/s sequential writes with a steady 600K random write IOPS, making short work of AI checkpoints. It gives ground at low and moderate queue depths, where QD1 writes and mixed workloads lag, and it ran warm on our bench.

Fast sequential and random writes.

Mixed-workload performance trails at middle QDs.

It has been revealed that why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

Phison is serious about enterprise storage, and the Pascari X201P was not released lightly; it came in the night, under NDA, alongside this week’s Supercomputing 2026 event. The drive is part of the Performance X-Series, which handles intensive workloads where consistency is the name of the game. We were nevertheless pleasantly surprised by its write performance, with a steady 12 GB/s for sequential and over 600,000 random write IOPS, considering it’s marketed at the 1 drive write per day (DWPD) endurance point.

Part of that surprise comes from the fact that this is Phison’s read-intensive PCIe 5.0 data center drive, a successor to the X200P. It comes in the U.2 form factor — which can be more convenient in many cases — from 1.92TB to 30.72TB, and an E3.S version from 3.84TB, in both single- and dual-port models. It stands next to its mixed-use sibling, the X201E, which is the one rated for 3 DWPD. What makes the X201P exciting, in part, is its own 16-channel X2 controller and the flash that’s inside.

It has been revealed that this drive is aimed at AI, analytics, and database servers, with its case made in the 4K 70/30 mix at higher queue depths. It passed Phison’s one-million-IOPS mark at QD128 in our testing of the 15.36TB model, and the drive met all of its rated specs, though its random read rating required polled I/O to reach on our bench. It faced challenges with QD1 writes, log commits, and the middle range of our mixed sweeps. Given its blend of performance, capacity, and endurance, we consider it a very competent entry from the organization that was perhaps better known in the consumer SSD market until recently.

According to recent reports, the drive met or beat every rated performance figure that we can test, which should be the target of any enterprise SSD released today. If there’s an exception, it’s due to how we test; Phison lists a ceiling of 3,250K IOPS for 4K random read, which is higher than our bench allows with our interrupt-driven I/O, which we use rather than a polled approach. We also run a polled test on every drive for cases like this, and our result was 3,283K IOPS at the same queue depth Phison specifies, which shows the drive does exceed its specification.

Datacenter NVMe SSD v2.0, with v2.6 telemetry features.

PCIe 5.0 x4, single port (2x2 dual-port models offered).

ISE, SED (TCG Opal 2.02) or non-SED; AES-XTS 256-bit.

Cryptographic erase and block erase.

512-byte and 4,096-byte, each with optional metadata.

Six: 25 W, 22 W, 20 W, 18 W, 15 W and 12 W maximum.

Host-controlled thermal management supported.

Seven; activation without reset.

NVMe-MI 1.2 over SMBus and PCIe.

Our sample is in the U.2 form factor, 15mm thick. We have the single-port SKU, ISE model XP208H0815T3P3216T310, with firmware X2WM6026. Some data we previously saw from the drive was reportedly on X2WM6025, but we confirmed X2WM6026 for all relevant results. We mounted the drive on a PCIe 5.0 x4 add-in card adapter for U.2, standing upright in the slot.

Phison did not provide firm hardware details, but we were able to discover some things on our own. The flash was probably the easiest, as the company claimed it was a 321-layer part. That can only be SK hynix’s V9 TLC, which is not flash we’ve tested before in any product. It’s exceptionally fast and uses a three-deck design, which is relatively upcoming for TLC flash. The flash could be credited with some of the exceptional performance measurements we see on the drive.

As for the proprietary controller, we’ve heard that it’s using a combination of the standard Arm Cortex-R5 — these would be the main cores — with AndesCore RISC-V on the side. We’ve seen the latter before on the Phison E28 consumer SSD controller, which did have some enterprise-like aspects to it. The E28 is the newer design, built on a 6nm process with Andes’ newer N45 cores alongside the N25F, while the X2 is a 12nm part that, as far as we can tell, sticks with N25F-class co-processors.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Sources indicate that in this case, the X2 has twice the flash channels, which enables a superior level of performance out of TLC flash, as in enterprise you do not rely on pSLC. That mix of cores sets the X2 apart from other 16-channel PCIe 5.0 enterprise controllers: Marvell’s Bravera SC5 and Silicon Motion’s SM8366 rely on Arm cores throughout, whereas Phison pairs its Cortex-R5 cores with small RISC-V co-processors.

Smart home tech often relies solely on cloud connections and pricey AI subscriptions, but UGREEN is delivering a local-first solution in its new HomeAgent collection, delivering cameras, speakers, and more that bring the bulk of the functionality and processing directly to your home.

The UGREEN AIoT – AI of Things – ecosystem is built around pairing hardware to a central hub that acts as your home’s brain. The HomeAgent HA100 and Pro are that “brain,” pairing to smart home gear such as lights, speakers, and cameras to not only store recordings, but process the data locally.

In a recent development, at the core of the experience is UGREEN’s Uliya AI assistant, which you can talk to directly through HomeAgent HA100 or through a connected Smart Speaker for Uliya. The assistant can handle simple tasks like controlling lights or playing music, of course, but can do a lot more with video recordings. You can ask questions such as “is there a package outside” or “where is my dog” and Uliya will be able to parse through camera recordings to find the answer rather than forcing you to have to scroll through timelines.

That’s all powered by the HomeAgent HA100. It can also acts as network storage for photos, household files, and more, all of which can be used as context for the local AI system – and there’s no monthly fee to store or access it.

UGREEN’s hardware lineup around the HomeAgent centerpieces includes cameras such as the SynCare cameras. These deliver the local recording capabilities that are so central to the system. SynCare OD800 Pro is a triple-lens outdoor camera with solar power and a built-in battery, while the OD600 Pro delivers the same powerful camera setup with power-over-ethernet. These have an 8MP primary camera and dual 5MP cameras with pan-tilt-zoom capabilities. They can zoom in up to 9x, feature motion tracking and a built-in spotlight, as well as color night vision and IP66 dust/water protection.

It has been revealed that meanwhile, the SynCare Indoor Cam ID500 Pro is a pan-tilt-zoom camera meant to be used inside to capture events in an entire room. It features 4K imaging, 360-degree pan and 160-degree vertical tilt while supporting up to 8x digital zoom, motion tracking, and even baby-cry detection. It also has a physical shutter for your privacy.

There are also two smart frames, the UGREEN Gallery E-Paper Smart Frame mounts on the wall to display photos and artwork, while the UGREEN Gallery LCD Smart Frame can sit on a table or hang on the wall, showing photos and videos, while also integrating with the rest of your smart home’s functions.

UGREEN has its own smart speaker for the system, and you can also integrate select Matter hardware as well, including smart lighting, robot vacuums and other smart home devices.

The UGREEN HomeAgent ecosystem will start at $799 for a limited time when its Kickstarter campaign launches on April 13, 2027, with upgraded packages that drastically increase AI processing power, storage, and the types of devices you can connect to the system.

According to recent reports, you can reserve your UGREEN HomeAgent today to lock in early bird pricing. Reservations are open from September 4, 2026, through April 12, 2027, and deposits can be canceled for a refund any time before the campaign ends. Shipping will begin in late June 2027, with different phases for different products.

Recent findings suggest that megaspeed was added to Nvidia's no-sell list in June 2025, the statement reveals, but a Upcoming York Times report claims that a Malaysian Megaspeed subsidiary continued to receive large shipments of Nvidia chips for a full eight months after that date. It's believed that Nvidia's export-controlled Blackwell and H200 chips were shipped to Speedmatrix, either via third parties or directly from Nvidia itself, before being handed off to China. Nvidia has argued that it was given Commerce Department permission to ship the components to Megaspeed. Notably, Nvidia continues to list Megaspeed as a cloud partner.

Sources indicate that the new criminal investigation follows a Commerce Department investigation into Megaspeed that first kicked off in 2024 over possible export violations. By May 2025, it had requested Nvidia's data relating to sales it made to Megaspeed, and by June, officials visited Megaspeed and even interviewed Alice Huang, the now-former executive who is allegedly a Chinese spy. Ms. Huang is also the woman that then-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with before resigning his position earlier this month. Following that visit, the Justice Department took the lead in the investigation into Megaspeed.

It has been revealed that joint Statement from Department of Commerce and Department of Justice on Megaspeed Investigation. https://t.co/aAdtN9aDfFNovember 17, 2026.

Megaspeed has long been accused of being a front for an AI component smuggling operation. In October 2025, an investigation claimed that it had helped move around $2 billion worth of Nvidia chips into China by importing them and then re-exporting them to the country. Megaspeed indicates that it complies with all laws and that the woman at the center of the affair scandal, Ms. Huang, is no longer at the company. The Chinese government has also dismissed claims that she was a state spy.

According to recent reports, the joint Commerce and Justice Departments' statement pointed to its strong track record when prosecuting chip smugglers to date. 17 defendants across a total of six investigations have been charged so far, with more likely to follow. A Californian man was recently arrested after being accused of smuggling more than $300 million worth of export-restricted Nvidia chips to China. He now faces up to 20 years in prison.

Recent findings suggest that elementor made your site easy to build. It may also be making it slow. Here's how to move a site onto the Block Editor without breaking URLs, losing content or dropping out of Google.

Recent findings suggest that page builders solved a real problem. Before the Block Editor matured, they were the easiest way to give clients drag-and-drop layouts. Many of those sites are still running today, and a lot of them are slow on phones.

The data backs that up. According to the HTTP Archive Core Web Vitals Technology Report for June 2026, 36.8% of Elementor sites pass Core Web Vitals on mobile. Sites built with the Block Editor pass 53.0% of the time. That's correlation, not proof, since hosting and setup matter too. But in my experience, it matches what happens when you remove the builder from a slow site.

It has been revealed that my reason for migrating sites off Elementor is simple: **page builders make websites heavy. **Having noted that, Elementor has improved a lot. Its performance settings, Flexbox Containers, and asset-loading options cut much of the bloat, and a carefully tuned Elementor site can pass Core Web Vitals. But tuning only goes so far. You’re still shipping the builder’s framework, wrapper markup and scripts, and every plugin or Elementor upgrade is a chance for the speed to slip again.

For small business sites that don’t need drag-and-drop editing, rebuilding the same design on the WordPress Block Editor (Gutenberg) removes that weight at the source, without changing what the client sees.

This guide follows the order I use. It assumes you're comfortable with WordPress admin, WP-CLI and a staging site. If you need to set those up first, SitePoint's guide to the ultimate WordPress development environment covers the tooling.

Not every Elementor site needs to move. Migration makes sense when:.

In a recent development, it's harder to justify when the site leans on Elementor Pro features you'd need to replace, such as complex popups, dynamic loops or WooCommerce templates. Those can all be rebuilt, but the job gets bigger fast.

You can't prove a migration worked without "before" numbers. Capture these on the live site first.

Industry observers note that crawl the site with a tool such as Screaming Frog, and export every indexable URL with its title, meta description, H1 and canonical tag. You can also pull published pages and posts with WP-CLI:.

In a recent development, run Google PageSpeed Insights, which uses Lighthouse for its lab scores, on the homepage and two or three key templates. Save the mobile lab scores and, if the site has enough traffic, the field data from real users.

In a recent development, export the last three months of pages and queries from Google Search Console. That's what you'll compare against after launch.

Elementor stores each page's layout as JSON in the elementordata post meta field, and marks builder pages with elementoredit_mode. This command lists every page that uses the builder:.

Then list everything else Elementor controls, which is easy to miss:.

On the small business sites I've migrated, the inventory usually turns up more than the owner expects. The pages are the easy part. The surprises are saved templates nobody remembers creating, a popup still running on every page, add-on widgets from plugins that were installed once and forgotten, and contact forms that live inside Elementor Pro rather than a form plugin. Finding those before the rebuild saves a broken launch.

Industry observers note that work on a staging copy. Install a block theme, such as Twenty Twenty-Five or a lightweight starter theme, and move the Elementor global styles into theme.json. That way colors, fonts and spacing are defined once, instead of in every widget.

Copy the hex values and font names from Elementor's Site Settings so the upcoming site matches the old one. Rebuild the header and footer as template parts in the Site Editor. If you'd rather write a theme yourself, SitePoint's series on building a WordPress theme from scratch covers the basics.

Most Elementor sites repeat the same few sections: a hero, a services grid, testimonials and a call to action. Build each one once as a block pattern, then reuse it on every page. Patterns are plain block markup, so you don't need React to write them, whatever you may have heard about React and WordPress development.

In a block theme, any PHP file in the /patterns folder with a header comment is registered automatically:.

Industry observers note that for page content, there's a useful shortcut. Elementor saves a plain HTML copy of each page into post_content. Open a page in the Block Editor, and the old content usually appears in a Classic block. Choose Convert to blocks, then delete the leftovers and rebuild the layout with your patterns. It keeps the copy and images, so you only redo the design.

Recent findings suggest that the difference highlights up in the page source. Here's typical front-end markup for a single heading on an Elementor page, using the older section and column layout:.

And the same heading as a block:.

Newer Elementor versions with Flexbox containers and the optimized markup settings trim some of those wrappers, but most older sites still carry all of them. Multiply that by every element on every page, and the weight adds up.

To speed up this step, I built a free Elementor to Gutenberg converter. Paste in a page's elementordata JSON from Step 2, and it returns block markup you can paste into the Block Editor's code editor. It handles headings, text, images, buttons, spacers, dividers and column layouts, and lists anything it can't convert, such as forms and popups, for you to rebuild by hand. It runs entirely in your browser, so the page data never leaves your computer.

Industry observers note that the code is rarely what holds a migration up. Content is. Once clients see their site being rebuilt, many decide it's time to rewrite their pages too, and the project ends up waiting on copywriters and approvals. My fix is to separate the two: migrate the existing content as it is, launch, then enhancement the copy afterwards. That keeps the speed and SEO gains on schedule, and it means any ranking change can be traced to either the migration or the new copy, not both at once.

This is the step that decides whether rankings hold.

To spot-check a redirect or a status code from the command line:.

Industry observers note that when staging matches the live site, deploy it. Then:.

According to recent reports, leave the old elementordata meta in place for a few weeks, in case you need to roll back. Once you're confident, take a backup and remove it to shrink the database.

Run PageSpeed Insights again straight away for lab scores. Field data takes longer: the Chrome UX Report uses a rolling 28-day window, so give it a month before judging real-user results. Compare Search Console clicks for the same period before and after launch.

In my migrations, the biggest change is usually page weight and loading time, because the builder's CSS, JavaScript and wrapper markup are gone. What doesn't always improve is server response time. If the site is on slow shared hosting, the first byte still arrives late, and that needs a hosting fix, not a rebuild. Search traffic should hold steady if the URLs and metadata were protected. If it drops, the Step 5 crawl comparison is the first place to look.

Moving off Elementor isn't a one-click job, but it isn't a full redesign either. Record a baseline, inventory what the builder controls, rebuild with patterns, and protect every URL. Most of the speed gain comes from removing code the site never needed. For what to tackle after that, see these practical web performance techniques. Most of the risk comes from rushing the SEO checks. Done carefully, the client gets the same site, a faster one, and an editor that comes with WordPress itself.

According to recent reports, first appearing earlier this month, Google Pixel phones are rolling out a handy new Family feature in the Settings menu. Here’s what it can do.

Rolling out now via what appears to be a server-side patch (tied to Google Play Services), Google Pixel phones are adding a “Family” section to the Settings menu. The feature is appearing for us on a Pixel 11 Pro XL running the October 2026 update (not Android 17 QPR2), while a Pixel 10 Pro has also just surfaced the latest UI.

It has been revealed that this upcoming section, which Google has previously referred to as “Family Hub,” gives customers a quick place to see their family members and settings in one central location. It shows a list of your family members – child accounts and anyone attached to your Google One family strategy – with controls over Google One storage, Google Play Family Library, shared payment methods, and “Family events” in Google Calendar.

You can also see the live location of any family members you are sharing your location with or start sharing your location with another family member. You can also easily remove or add members to your family plan via this newly introduced menu. Each family member gets their own page where you can see benefits shared, location, and also if they are a “parent” in the family – with “remove” and “transfer” options available.

I've had it for a few weeks, and while it's surely something useful for those with a "family setup", it's IMHO a major annoyance for those who don't (who, I suspect, are the vast majority).

Couldn't they have it show up only for those "in a family"?

It's there, at the top, doing absolutely nothing useful for the vast majority of people, and pushing down all other options.

While this won’t be helpful for all customers, it’s certainly full of useful shortcuts and tools for those at the center of a family strategy and looking to share benefits with their household.

Recent findings suggest that as far as we can tell, this is widely rolled out to Pixel owners at this point. As mentioned, we’re seeing it across multiple devices, and 9to5Google readers mentioned they’re also seeing it live even prior to installing the latest system enhancement. The folks at Droid-Life also mention now seeing it on their Pixels.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • CNBC reports that Nvidia has started warning its customers that impending legislation to clamp down on countries accessing AI GPUs remotely via data center rentals could put them in trouble with U.S.
  • According to the report, Nvidia has been messaging chip buyers to warn that RASA could expose both Nvidia and chip buyers to legal risk.
  • House of Representatives has already passed a bill called the Remote Access Security Act (RASA) that addressed this specific loophole, but it’s been in limbo in the Senate for over ten months now.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

CNBC reports that Nvidia has started warning its customers that impending legislation to clamp down on countries accessing AI GPUs remotely via data center rentals could put them in trouble with U.S. authorities. Chinese tech companies could take advantage of the performance of American AI hardware through a loophole in U.S. regulations. Instead of importing Nvidia chips, which are under export controls, they instead look to data centers located abroad and export their data instead. This is what Chinese AI lab Moonshot is apparently trying in Europe, which is why the U.S. Department of Commerce, through the Bureau of Industry and Security [PDF], released an interim final rule closing this loophole.

According to the report, Nvidia has been messaging chip buyers to warn that RASA could expose both Nvidia and chip buyers to legal risk.

The U.S. House of Representatives has already passed a bill called the Remote Access Security Act (RASA) that addressed this specific loophole, but it’s been in limbo in the Senate for over ten months now. It remains unclear if the Jensen Huang affair and suspected espionage scandal will help speed up its approval, but scheduling could be tight with only about 31 calendar days remaining before the Senate's adjournment. But even before any of these regulations are approved and published, the organization is already taking steps to protect its customers and has started requiring partners that 51% of their services should go to non-Chinese clients. It has also required its partners to join Nvidia’s Fleet Intelligence tracking system if they want to retain their official partner status.

It’s unclear if these changes have been planned over time or were a reaction to the renewed scrutiny that Nvidia is facing. But even though Jensen Huang is now out of the company, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent remarked that it’s unclear if the former Nvidia CEO was aware of the alleged smuggling operations and instead laid the blame on the entire company. Nvidia itself has taken steps to improve its security and export control teams by establishing an oversight committee that will be in charge of its “national security policies, export control compliance, and global trade risk management,” and would work with third-party experts in law, national security, and trade compliance.

These measures would further tighten the noose around China’s AI GPUs. Even though it has several domestic chip makers, many AI operators still prefer Nvidia chips for their performance and reliability. There have even been allegations that Alibaba and ByteDance, some of China’s biggest tech companies, prefer training their LLMs in Southeast Asia to bypass bans and restrictions. So, if the U.S. finally shuts down this loophole, we can expect these companies to scramble and find a replacement for the Nvidia GPUs they could access right now.

Pixel Tag is a brilliant Band-Aid on a Find Hub network Google can’t easily fix

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (835 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5google

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the Google Pixel Tag is here and, at least so far, it’s really good.
  • It has been revealed that the good news on Pixel Tag: this is a well-built tracker that, unlike others, is the clear product of the hardware having direct access to the software.
  • Google’s Find Hub network has improved dramatically over the two years since its launch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the Google Pixel Tag is here and, at least so far, it’s really good. But fresh hardware and some newly introduced features can’t fix the core problem. Google’s Find Hub network has been restricted from the very start, and it’s not something Google can easily fix.

It has been revealed that the good news on Pixel Tag: this is a well-built tracker that, unlike others, is the clear product of the hardware having direct access to the software. Little touches like being able to adjust ringer volume on the fly combine nicely with UWB – the latter something we rarely see on third-party devices largely due to Apple – all things that elevate the Find Hub tracker to what we called the new “gold standard.”.

The bad news: this is still a Find Hub tracker.

Google’s Find Hub network has improved dramatically over the two years since its launch. Where Google originally had to admit that tracking performance was lacking (a nice way of putting it, frankly), improvements started arriving in 2025. We noticed that the network seemed to be working much better a few months after its wide rollout, and Google later confirmed speed improvements.

But, ultimately, the Find Hub network is still reeling from how it debuted.

In a recent development, google had a privacy focus when launching what was originally called the “Find My Device” network, defaulting the network to only be active on Android phones in “high-traffic areas” only. People could switch this to “all areas,” but the initial rollout defaulted to effectively cutting off anywhere that wasn’t a major metro, airport/travel hub, etc. It left the network useless to many. Google defended this as a “first-of-its-kind safety protection,” but I’d argue it hindered the network into a state of inefficacy.

According to recent reports, again, it’s gotten better since then, but it’s still not as good as it should be. Samsung’s network, limited solely to Galaxy phones, shouldn’t outperform Google’s. Find Hub trackers should be just as good as AirTags and the third-party trackers that work with Apple’s network. They’re just not, and I truly do believe it all boils down to this initial choice. One of the reasons this is getting better is that Google has been pushing users to the “all areas” setting during the setup of a upcoming device – I’ve noticed this on some recent devices I set up, but it’s not been completely consistent just yet. That’s a good step forward but, even if it is the new default, that still requires millions of users to upgrade their devices, and we’ve never been in a better time to not upgrade your phone.

Recent findings suggest that all of that is to say, the Pixel Tag isn’t fixing this problem. Surely, it’ll give Google some needed fire to fix the problem, but new hardware isn’t the solution. That’s something I was discussing with 9to5Google readers on our review. UWB is a tentpole feature of the Pixel Tag, but it doesn’t change the network problems, it just improves precision finding. We needed a first-party tracker like this regardless of the state of the network, something that really takes advantage of the platform and pushes it forward, but it’s just a quick fix, a Band-Aid.

What do you think? Have you found the Find Hub network reliable enough, or is there still room for improvement? Sound off in the comments below!

It has been revealed that after years of waiting, Rockstar's Grand Theft Auto 6 is finally here, and it's already astonishing players with its immaculately detailed environments, unexpected celebrity cameos, and absurdly interactive NPCs. Much like Leonida's various radio stations play all-time bangers and deep cuts, GTA 6 is also packed with references to memorable memes and pop-culture moments, and many of them are easy to miss. For instance, the game contains an homage to a hilarious viral moment from E3 2006, and it's not even a full-on side quest but a random discovery you'll stumble upon as you explore GTA 6's intricate open world.

Recent findings suggest that while the unexpected appearance of a very large crustacean is noteworthy in its own right, "giant enemy crabs" have a special meaning in the world of video games. Back in 2006, during Sony's E3 presentation, one of the developers of Genji 2 explained that the game's stages were based on actual battles that took place in ancient Japan, with hundreds of warriors on either side. Sounds quite gritty and rooted in historical realism, right? Turns out, "based on" is doing some heavy lifting here, because in addition to ordinary men, you'll also be fighting "giant enemy crabs.".

In a recent development, there is sadly little in the historical record to suggest that Japan's coastlines were populated by giant crabs at any point in its history, "ancient" or otherwise. Even so, the cringiness of the presentation made it a viral phenomenon on mid-00s YouTube, inspiring several remixes and blog posts. It even inspired a fan-made Flash browser game. In the years since, the "giant enemy crab" has been lovingly referenced in tons of other games, including League of Legends, Vampire Survivors, Borderlands, Viva Pinata, and Astro Bot. Two decades later, the gag's made it all the way to the biggest video game of all time.

Grand Theft Auto 6 is out now for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X.

#46792. AMD attacks Nvidia's FP64 emulation at SC26, touts native double-precision on Instinct MI430X

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (930 w)
📖 Baca
Hardware & Chips ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Tomshardware ↗ Open Full Page

AMD attacks Nvidia's FP64 emulation at SC26, touts native double-precision on Instinct MI430X

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (930 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As Supercomputing 2026 (SC26) opens in Chicago this week, AMD is indirectly needling Nvidia about the lack of native FP64 data type support in its data center GPU products.
  • Over the past few years, Nvidia has reallocated die area on its data center GPUs to favor the lower-precision matrix math that boosts the operations needed for much of modern AI inference.
  • According to recent reports, to make up for the lack of native FP64 support, Nvidia has turned to techniques that allow it to emulate FP64 operations using methods like the Ozaki schemes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As Supercomputing 2026 (SC26) opens in Chicago this week, AMD is indirectly needling Nvidia about the lack of native FP64 data type support in its data center GPU products. FP64, or double-precision floating-point math, is widely used in the high-performance scientific computing and simulation fields that are the focus of SC26. For those customers, AMD is trumpeting the value of its latest Instinct MI430X accelerator for customers that still need native FP64, like national laboratories and supercomputing centers.

Over the past few years, Nvidia has reallocated die area on its data center GPUs to favor the lower-precision matrix math that boosts the operations needed for much of modern AI inference. That reallocation only makes business sense, as the total addressable market for AI compute has exploded while the demand for double-precision math in large supercomputing installations has remained flat by comparison.

According to recent reports, to make up for the lack of native FP64 support, Nvidia has turned to techniques that allow it to emulate FP64 operations using methods like the Ozaki schemes. But AMD claims this kind of emulation is nowhere close to a replacement for native double-precision processing for a few reasons—hence continued development of specialized products like the MI430X.

For one, AMD notes that Ozaki emulation assumes that the workload in question resembles a dense general matrix multiply (GEMM). In its own application profiling, the company says "less than 10%" of HPC workloads perform dense GEMM operations, so this emulation is a good replacement for native compute. Dense linear algebra is the one common workload for which AMD says Ozaki emulation is a natural fit.

For workloads like sparse iterative linear algebra, stencils and hydrodynamics, high-order finite element analysis, Monte Carlo and particle transport, and classical molecular dynamics, AMD says developers still need strong FP64 vector performance for the best results.

Sources indicate that furthermore, even for workloads that map well onto GEMM operations, AMD says matrix sizes must be large in order to achieve the best performance, and that might also not be a given for every operation. The operands of those matrices also have to be sized well to the hardware, as incorrectly scaled operands can reduce performance. The FP64 vector math capabilities of the MI430X are insensitive to those operand sizing issues.

Beyond those stumbling blocks, AMD also notes that using Ozaki emulation methods can cause the memory footprint of an application to balloon, requiring up to three times more capacity than native FP64 would.

Since HBM capacity is directly tied to GPUs in modern supercomputing installations, fitting a workload to a machine that can only emulate FP64 operations could have cascading effects on the number of GPUs and compute nodes required, causing knock-on challenges for the floor area, power, and cooling required to support the system.

AMD notes the high 432GB of HBM4 memory capacity per MI430X node allows its customers to provision fewer GPUs and compute nodes in a system, saving on networking, power, and floor space.

In addition to its FP64 HPC performance, AMD positions an MI430X-powered supercomputer as an AI inference platform for developing workloads that utilize those models as part of the research process. But there are some key differences between those systems and the Helios rack-scale accelerator powered by MI455X GPUs from the same CDNA 5 architectural family.

Each MI430X GPU offers 9.2 PFLOPS of theoretical FP4 compute performance for inference, but that should be understood in the context of the whopping 40.3 PFLOPS of FP4 compute from each AI-focused MI455X accelerator.

Beyond raw performance, the native scale-up domain size of four MI430Xs over AMD’s Infinity Fabric interconnect when coupled with a sixth-generation EPYC host CPU pales in comparison to the domain size of 72 MI455X accelerators in a Helios rack. AMD claims this interconnect is optimized more for latency-sensitive operations rather than a massive scale-up domain.

Of course, every customer and user of such a system will have different requirements, and institutional supercomputing installations usually aren’t trying to do double duty as cloud inference providers.

For scientists and engineers whose AI models of choice work well within the 1.72 TB of aggregate HBM4 capacity and 93.2 TB/s of memory bandwidth offered by four MI430X's working together across the 12.3 Tbps of scale-up bandwidth available within such a node, the inference performance of each node is likely more than up to the task of the kinds of AI applications that need to be run alongside double-precision compute workloads.

In any event, the MI430X can already count several supercomputing design wins in its corner. The upcoming Discovery supercomputer at Oak Ridge National Laboratory, the Alice Recoque installation in France, the LUMI-AI system at Finland’s CSC, and the Herder system in Germany will all take advantage of the native FP64 support offered by the MI430X.

AMD’s continued support for native FP64, even as Nvidia retreats from that capability in its products, will doubtless be a point of pride for its architects and engineers, even as those institutional supercomputers will be dwarfed by both AMD and Nvidia-powered AI inference installations the world over. The firm's semi-custom silicon design chops and chiplet experience give it the flexibility needed to tailor products like the MI430X to these specialized markets instead of pursuing a one-size-fits-all approach.

In a recent development, as the Senior Analyst, Graphics at Tom's Hardware, Jeff Kampman covers everything that has to do with graphics cards, gaming performance, and more. From integrated graphics processors to discrete graphics cards to the hyperscale installations powering our AI future, if it's got a GPU in it, Jeff is on it.

Following the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, a Taiwanese skyscraper became the backdrop for a series of messages in support of the ousted founder, who admitted to having an affair with a woman who has been accused of being a spy for the Chinese government. The U.S. government has since announced a criminal investigation into the tech giant the woman worked for, Megaspeed, over concerns it may have aided in the breaking of export controls related to Nvidia AI chips. Despite that fact, CNA reports that the Taipei 101 building saw messages projected onto its exterior on the night of November 16. The messages included “Taiwan ♡ Jensen,” “Family ♡ Friendship,” and “Thrive Together,” with the driving force likely to be Huang's almost celebrity-like level of fame in the country.

That celebrity status has seen public sympathy for Huang grow within Taiwan, with people within the country's technology industry coming together to fund the project. One technology worker reportedly said that the light show was supposed to “bring back Jensen Huang” and show Taiwan's concern.

Industry observers note that that concern may not be needed for too much longer. Recent reports suggest that Huang could be plotting a return to the top job at Nvidia just days after he handed in his resignation. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney have already thrown their weight behind the idea of Huang's return to Nvidia. The clamor to force the hand of Nvidia's board has also extended to the White House, with U.S. President Trump also calling for the former CEO to be reinstated. This is despite ongoing uncertainty over whether his love interest was a Chinese spy and, if so, how much Huang may have known about that fact. Trump, however, says that Huang did not put national security at risk.

For its part, it isn't believed that the Nvidia board is seriously considering allowing Huang to pick up where he left off pre-resignation. A source told CNBC that the organization is focused on investigating Huang's conduct and a national security investigation and is not discussing his return. That investigation will no doubt also consider reports that Huang had another affair, this time with an Nvidia executive.

For now, Nvidia's former CFO Colette Kress is serving as interim CEO. Kress hasn't had long to settle in ahead of the first substantial test — the company's first earnings call since the scandal will take place today, November 17.

Ahead of the holiday season, Google Maps is launching a handy travel itineraries feature alongside a slew of other newly introduced capabilities for Ask Maps.

Ask Maps can now build travel itineraries that feature numbered map pins for each stop. It supports everything from shopping excursions to multi-day road trips with several stops. When used for the latter, Google Maps will generate a day-by-day schedule with tips and the numbered pins that aid visualization. Intends can be shared with others and exported to Google Docs on desktop.

Once on the trip, Ask Maps will show directions and real-time details, including live traffic conditions, whether a place is open, and “even what the vibe is at your next stop.” You can conversationally have Google add more stops to the itinerary.

In a recent development, meanwhile, Ask Maps can now tap into your saved lists to find bookmarked places and take action. This lets you ask: “Which spots saved in my lists have availability for five people in the next 30 minutes?”.

Before you start directions, you’ll see familiar “Know Before You Go” tips that surface information about your route, like parking locations, car charging options, weather, potential delays, and tolls.

Latest agentic capabilities let Ask Maps find online beauty, pet care, auto, and home repair appointments, as well as call local businesses on your behalf. For example, “Find me a 4 p.m. nail appointment near me” returns a list of open slots.

Finally, Ask Maps is expanding to 30 more countries across Europe, including Spain, Germany, and the UK.

In a recent development, these updates are rolling out starting today on Google Maps for Android and iOS. Travel itineraries and list search are available in all 200+ Ask Maps countries. Know Before You Go in directions and appointment booking are coming first to the US.

It has been revealed that sending a document for signature is the easy part of an e-signature integration. One POST request and the signer gets an email. The work that actually breaks in production happens afterwards: knowing when the document was signed, trusting the notification that told you so, handling the same notification twice, and getting the final PDF into storage before the download link expires.

Sources indicate that this tutorial builds that whole loop in Node.js with Express. An event in your app (a deal is approved, a client is onboarded, a task moves to "ready to sign") sends a contract from a template. When the signer finishes, a webhook arrives, your server verifies it, and the signed PDF plus its audit trail get saved without anyone touching them.

The code uses Firma.dev, the e-signature API I work on, because I needed a real API to make the examples runnable. The patterns are not specific to it, though. Signature verification, idempotent handlers, short-lived download URLs, and reconciliation jobs show up in almost every webhook-driven integration, and the same structure applies whether you're receiving events from a payment processor, a CI system, or another signing provider.

There's a fifth part that tutorials usually skip: a reconciliation job that catches anything the webhooks missed. We'll build that too, because webhooks are a notification mechanism, not a delivery guarantee.

Set three environment variables:.

It has been revealed that before sending anything, wrap the HTTP calls in one place. This is where authentication lives, and it's also where you handle 429 Too Many Requests once instead of in every caller. Most APIs, this one included, return a Retry-After header on a 429, so the client should honour it rather than guessing a backoff.

According to recent reports, the 503 branch matters later. When a document has just been completed, the final PDF and its completion certificate take a moment to generate, and the download endpoint indicates so with a 503 and a Retry-After instead of handing you a half-built file.

According to recent reports, the trigger depends on your product. It might be a route handler, a queue consumer, or a CRM automation calling into your service. What matters is that the function doing the sending is small and takes plain data:.

Two design choices are worth calling out.

Sources indicate that use a single create-and-send call when you can. Many signing APIs split this into "create a draft" and "send the draft." That's useful when a human needs to review the document first, but for automation it creates a window where your process can crash between the two calls and leave an orphaned draft. A combined endpoint makes the operation atomic from your side.

Store the provider's ID on your own record immediately. Webhook payloads reference the signing request, not your deal or customer. Without that mapping you'll end up searching by email address, which falls apart as soon as one client signs two documents.

According to recent reports, here's the first place integrations quietly go wrong. Webhook signatures are computed over the exact bytes the sender transmitted. If Express parses the body as JSON first, you lose those bytes, and re-serialising the object won't reproduce them (key order, whitespace, and number formatting can all change). Signature checks then fail intermittently, which is the worst kind of failure.

The fix is to use express.raw() on the webhook route only, so the handler receives a Buffer:.

Sources indicate that most webhook providers sign payloads with HMAC-SHA256 using a shared secret. The details vary, so read your provider's docs for the exact header format, but the scheme here is common: the header looks like t=1731456000,v1=5f2b..., and the signed string is the timestamp, a dot, and the raw body. Stripe uses a very similar format, and the Standard Webhooks spec describes the same idea as a vendor-neutral convention.

Each line here defends against something specific.

The OWASP guidance on cryptographic storage covers the other half of this: the secret belongs in an environment variable or secrets manager, never in the repository.

According to recent reports, every serious webhook system delivers at least once, not exactly once. If your endpoint is slow, returns a 5xx, or the network drops the response, the sender retries. Firma.dev, for example, makes up to three attempts per event (immediately, then after at least five minutes, then after at least an hour) and treats anything other than a 2xx as a failure, including redirects. Other providers retry more aggressively. Either way, your handler will eventually see the same event twice.

The defence is to record each event's unique ID and skip ones you've seen. In the server above that's alreadyProcessed and markProcessed. For a demo, a Set works:.

In production, use your database and let a unique constraint do the work, so two concurrent deliveries can't both pass the check:.

According to recent reports, also notice the order in the route: respond with 200, then do the work. Many providers time out deliveries after a few seconds (five, in this case). Downloading a PDF and uploading it to object storage can easily take longer than that, and a timeout counts as a failure, which triggers a retry, which triggers duplicate work. Acknowledging fast and processing asynchronously avoids that loop.

Sources indicate that setImmediate is fine for a tutorial, but it has a real weakness: if the process dies after sending the 200 and before finishing the work, the event is acknowledged and lost. In production, push the event onto a durable queue (BullMQ, SQS, a jobs table) before responding. Step 7 covers the safety net for whatever still slips through.

According to recent reports, now the actual business logic. You'll usually see several event types (sent, viewed, a signer signed, declined, expired, completed). Only one of them means "the document is final":.

Three things in here are easy to get wrong.

Don't treat "a signer signed" as "the document is done." With multiple signers, each one triggers its own event, and a per-signer "all complete" flag can be true on more than one of them. Key your storage logic off the single completion event.

Don't persist the download URL. Pre-signed URLs expire (this one carries an expires_at). Saving the link to your database and serving it to users later produces broken links a few minutes or hours later. Download the bytes and store them in storage you control. Swapping the fs.writeFile calls for an S3 PutObject or a Google Drive upload is a drop-in change.

Sources indicate that store the audit trail, not just the PDF. If a signature is ever disputed, the PDF shows what was signed, and the audit trail shows who signed it, when, and from where (timestamps, IP addresses, the sequence of views and signatures). That evidence is what makes an electronic signature defensible, which brings us to the legal side.

According to recent reports, retries are finite. Endpoints go down during deploys. Some providers auto-disable a webhook after enough consecutive failures, and events aren't guaranteed to arrive in order. Any one of these can leave a completed document sitting unsaved.

Sources indicate that A small scheduled job closes that gap. Keep a list of signing requests your app considers "pending," and periodically ask the API for their real status:.

Since storeSignedDocument overwrites by ID, running it twice for the same document is harmless. That's the property you want from every step in a webhook pipeline: doing it again shouldn't change the result.

None of this is legal advice, but a few facts shape how you build.

In the US, the ESIGN Act and the Uniform Electronic Transactions Act (adopted by 49 states) give electronic signatures the same legal standing as handwritten ones for most commercial documents. ESIGN also has requirements around consumer consent and record retention, which is part of why you store the final PDF yourself rather than relying on a third-party link.

Industry observers note that in the EU, eIDAS defines three levels: simple (SES), advanced (AdES), and qualified (QES). SES and AdES cover most business contracts. QES requires a qualified trust service provider and certificate-based identity, and some documents (certain property transfers and court filings, depending on the country) require it or exclude e-signatures entirely. Check which level your document types need before you pick a provider, since not every API offers every level.

Across jurisdictions, the evidence that holds up is the same: who signed, how they were identified, when it happened, and proof the document hasn't changed since. That's the audit trail and the completion certificate, which is why Step 6 stores both.

If you're evaluating providers for a workflow like this, the questions that matter at the integration level are mostly not on the pricing page:.

Sources indicate that the send call is one line. The reliability comes from everything around it: keeping the raw body for verification, checking timestamps and comparing in constant time, acknowledging fast and deduplicating by event ID, downloading files before their links expire, and running a reconciliation job for the events that never arrive. Get those right and contract signing becomes something your app does in the background, with no one chasing signatures or copying PDFs between folders.

Nvidia claims it’s ‘absurd’ to assume it predicted the agentic moment during Vera’s development

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, one criticism that has emerged of Nvidia’s Vera CPU, driven by AMD, is that Nvidia – and, to a lesser degree, Arm with its AGI CPU – couldn’t have developed an “agentic CPU,” as the chip is often characterized in Nvidia’s marketing materials.
  • “There's a conviction around the design philosophy of the part, right?
  • Instead of specifically designing Vera for agentic workloads, which would be impossible without a way to see several years into the future, Finder characterized the part by its codesign with Nvidia’s accelerators, something that the team has continued to work on since its first Grace data center CPU.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, one criticism that has emerged of Nvidia’s Vera CPU, driven by AMD, is that Nvidia – and, to a lesser degree, Arm with its AGI CPU – couldn’t have developed an “agentic CPU,” as the chip is often characterized in Nvidia’s marketing materials. Ian Finder, the head of Nvidia’s data center CPU business, pushed back on that criticism in a recent conversation with Tom’s Hardware Premium at SC26, calling the notion that Nvidia somehow knew about the agentic wave four years ago when Vera development began "absurd.".

“There's a conviction around the design philosophy of the part, right? Am I going to sit here and tell you that we have this magic crystal ball around the agentic moment? That would be absurd, right?” Finder said. “But what we do have as a company, and I think this has been proven out in our track record, is [that] we have design intuition.”.

Instead of specifically designing Vera for agentic workloads, which would be impossible without a way to see several years into the future, Finder characterized the part by its codesign with Nvidia’s accelerators, something that the team has continued to work on since its first Grace data center CPU. Coming from the assumption that data centers and AI workloads are accelerated (and they largely are), Finder indicates the co-design approach on the CPU can start in a “conceptually simple space, like what kind of CPU do we need to keep the accelerator fed and happy?”.

According to recent reports, although conceptually simple, Finder continually looped back to a particular word to describe aspects of Vera and, to a lesser extent, Grace. “Opinionated” is the word he used, which in the broader context of Vera’s design, highlights up in two places. Grace, Finder says, introduced an opinionated memory system with Nvidia’s Scalable Coherency Fabric, while Vera extends that memory system while adding an opinionated microarchitecture, Nvidia’s Olympus core.

Industry observers note that the picture Finder paints is one of Nvidia starting from scratch in this space, contrasting it with the “legacy constraints” of, presumably, Intel and AMD in particular, who have large pools of customers with specific needs. As we described in our original breakdown of the Olympus architecture in Vera, Nvidia’s goal doesn’t seem to be to steal market share from AMD and Intel, but rather to grab market share in a CPU space that’s vastly accelerating on the back of AI agents.

Sources indicate that this “clean sheet of paper” approach, and Nvidia’s codesign, led to some natural assumptions about what the CPU should do. “If we have silicon that needs really, really great single-thread performance, [and] we also need concurrency, then we need to get there with IPC instead of frequency. We need to make sure we have good loaded memory latency. We need to make sure we have a lot of bandwidth, and you start to design something on a clean sheet of paper that's not encumbered by dollar-per-core economics.”.

Industry observers note that although Finder was clear that Vera’s design didn’t explicitly center around the agents we see today, there were early indications of the workload. “To say that four years ago, when we started putting pen to paper on Vera, [that] we absolutely saw the agentic moment, would [not] be... something I would claim, but we were starting to see the beginnings of tool calling and things like that. We certainly knew what we needed from a head node, and we knew the overall shape of this problem.”.

According to recent reports, as you can see in our Vera CPU benchmarking, the chip doesn’t excel at every workload. And, from the data you can see in our recent AMD EPYC Venice benchmarking, the AMD camp has reclaimed some top spots in several benchmarks. Finder suggests that the superior memory bandwidth of Vera will play a much bigger role in the agentic future as these systems evolve to take better advantage of the compute available.

In a recent development, A portion of the AI industry is focused on tackling the problem of fully utilizing the GPU, Nvidia included. GPUs shouldn’t sit idle for very long (if at all) with the demand today, and they don’t. The challenge today is spinning up these agent sandboxes swiftly, within milliseconds, so that the CPU isn’t sitting idle, either.

Finder provided an example of using a coding agent. If you’ve used a coding agent before, you’re probably familiar with this process. After prompting, the model will make several small tool calls to read and locate files, passing back to the model in between. These are tiny calls, almost negligible, and the vast majority of the time is spent in the model on the GPU. Then, it may start compiling and testing the project, which is much more bound by the CPU. The GPU, Finder says, isn't sitting idle during that time. It’s being leveraged for another purpose. Finder suggests “that very same thing is going to happen on the CPU.”.

Sources indicate that this “very interesting computer science problem,” as Finder described it, is being investigated by AI startups such as Daytona and E2B to spin up and close down agentic sandboxes in milliseconds. And serving more agents will naturally put pressure on the memory system, which is an area where Vera has an edge. “We built a product that does really, really well without such optimizations, but as a design point that really will lean into them when the industry starts to catch up to this,” Finder noted.

According to recent reports, vera is a fascinating chip, regardless of what you think of it and how it’s presented in marketing materials (from Nvidia itself or elsewhere). Although Grace was the starting point internally, Vera has ridden the wave of agentic to become a much bigger player in the world of CPUs, and Nvidia has already confirmed that it will follow up with its Rosa CPU featuring the new Rigel microarchitecture. Vera is an opinionated CPU indeed, and time will tell if that opinion is correct.

Jake Roach is the Senior CPU Analyst at Tom’s Hardware, writing reviews, news, and features about the latest consumer and workstation processors.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Skydance CEO David Ellison says the tech giant will honor the distribution deal to stream Alex Gibney’s Musk documentary, even after Elon Musk’s $1 billion investment in the company.
  • Skydance CEO David Ellison indicates the company will honor the distribution deal to stream Alex Gibney’s Musk documentary, even after Elon Musk’s $1 billion investment in the company.
  • The nearly four-hour documentary on the Tesla and SpaceX executive is expected to hit HBO Max in early 2027, but Musk’s recent investment had put into question whether the streamer would air it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Skydance CEO David Ellison says the tech giant will honor the distribution deal to stream Alex Gibney’s Musk documentary, even after Elon Musk’s $1 billion investment in the company. The nearly four-hour documentary on the Tesla and SpaceX executive is expected to hit HBO Max in early 2027, but Musk’s recent investment had put into question whether the streamer would air it. HBO is now part of Skydance following the controversial merger between Warner Bros. Discovery and Paramount earlier this year. While Bleecker Street Media holds the U.S. theatrical rights and Universal Pictures the international distribution rights, HBO has the North American streaming rights for the documentary. When asked about the potential conflict at the 2026 DealBook summit in Latest York on Wednesday, Ellison told New York Times columnist and DealBook founder Andrew Ross Sorkin that he intends to follow through with the commitment to A24. “We believe in independence. We don’t believe in censorship of any kind,” Ellison told Sorkin. He added: “We have that deal with A24, and of course we’ll honor it.”  According to Deadline, Ellison appears to have misattributed the deal to HBO’s pay-1 deal with A24, a multiyear licensing deal that gives HBO exclusive streaming rights to A24-made films. A pay-1 deal gives a premium cable network or streaming service the first window to exclusively air a film following its theatrical release. Pay-1 windows often last about 18 months, at which point other networks can acquire streaming rights. Deadline reports that the deal Ellison refers to is most likely a commitment with HBO Documentary Films instead. The statement from Ellison follows Musk’s own criticism of the documentary, which he referred to as a “hit piece.” The documentary in question features interviews with figures from Musk’s life, including his first wife, Justine Musk; Tesla cofounder Martin Eberhard; and Ashley St. Clair, the mother of Musk’s 13th child. Additionally, figures from the entrepreneur and tech world are also featured in the film, including LinkedIn cofounder Reid Hoffman and British Canadian computer scientist Geoffrey Hinton, also known as the “godfather of AI.” Ellison also took the stage to praise Musk, calling him “the greatest entrepreneur of our time.” He added: “To have his vote of confidence and to have him as a shareholder is an honor and a privilege. And if there was any opportunity to be able to collaborate with him in the future, from our perspective, it would be a privilege.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that it’s almost here: Anthropic is expected to go public on Thursday, November 19, and its IPO share price has been set well above the company’s target range, a sign that demand for the stock is strong. The AI giant, best known for its LLM Claude, is in the middle of the biggest—or at least the most-hyped—initial public offering since SpaceX went public in a record stock listing earlier this year. Late Wednesday, Anthropic confirmed that it priced shares at $83, above earlier estimates of $70 to $78 per share. Anthropic’s offering consists of 980 million shares of Class A common stock, with the company selling roughly 956.4 million shares itself and certain stockholders selling about 23.6 million. The Wall Street Journal, Bloomberg, and other media outlets reported the $83 share price earlier in the day. A lot is hinging on how well Anthropic’s stock performs in the public markets on Thursday as AI-related stocks have seen a significant pullback in the wake of escalating “AI bubble” fears compounded by the recent ouster of Nvidia’s Jensen Huang. Here’s what to know as Anthropic’s stock is about to commence trading. About Anthropic Anthropic, PBC (Nasdaq: ANT) is an artificial intelligence public benefit corporation based in San Francisco. It was established in January 2021 by a group of seven cofounders who left now-rival OpenAI over safety and direction concerns and disagreements. That includes Dario Amodei, CEO; Daniela Amodei, president; Tom Brown, chief compute officer; Jack Clark, head of public benefit; Jared Kaplan, chief science officer; Sam McCandlish, chief architect; and Chris Olah, interpretability research lead. Anthropic’s primary product is its Claude LLM, which itself has multiple tiers, and other features such as its AI assistant, its coding tool Claude Code, and more. What’s particularly notable about Anthropic’s IPO is that it may be considered one of the first and most valuable pure-play AI IPOs—meaning that Anthropic’s primary function and market is AI, while many other companies in the space (Microsoft, Amazon, Google, etc.) have broader business operations that include AI. Also notable is the company’s prospectus, which includes more than 90 pages of risk factors that investors should take into consideration. That list, it’s worth pointing out, also includes “existential risks” to humanity. When is Anthropic’s IPO? Anthropic shares are expected to start trading on November 19, when the stock market opens at 9:30 a.m. ET. The stock will trade under the ticker “ANT,” which was already at the top of Yahoo’s trending stock tickers list on Wednesday, despite not actively trading yet. A countdown clock on the ANT ticker page alerts customers to when trading is expected to begin—down to the second (although the actual time may differ). Anthropic shares will trade on the Nasdaq Global Select Market. What is the IPO share price of ANT? The initial public offering price for ANT shares is $83, higher than Anthropic’s projected range of $70 to $78 per share. How many ANT shares are available in its IPO? Anthropic’s initial public offering will include the sale of 980 million shares of its Class A common stock, above an earlier estimate of 825 million. The lead underwriters for Anthropic’s IPO are Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, per its prospectus. How much is Anthropic expected to raise in its IPO? Anthropic’s valuation is now as high as $1.5 trillion, Bloomberg estimates. That puts it on the cusp of the top 10 largest companies in the world by market capitalization; it could be worth more than Walmart and Berkshire Hathaway, for instance, and roughly on par with Tesla and Meta. Assuming it does reach a valuation of $1.5 trillion, Anthropic would be one of 15 public companies worth at least $1 trillion. What are analysts saying? As noted, Anthropic is the biggest pure-play AI IPO to come along, which has investors chomping at the bit. But it’s also rife with risks, as outlined in its prospectus and filing statements. The company is definitely driving revenue: Its S-1 filing highlights that through the first nine months of 2026, Anthropic saw revenue of $33.2 billion, up more than 1,200% year over year. Analysts generally have a rosy view of the stock ahead of the IPO. New Street Research rated it a “buy,” and analyst Pierre Ferragu called it a “generational IPO,” according to CNBC. KGI Securities likewise rated the stock as “buy,” and gave it a price target of $105, significantly higher than the pre-IPO range. Analysts at Morningstar set a target of $92 per share, also seeing the stock as “undervalued” ahead of trading. Disclosure: Morningstar was founded by Fast Company’s owner, Joe Mansueto. This developing story has been updated.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The “Android Time Machine” is a fun project that puts Android versions into your browser, giving you a quick and easy chance to play around with older versions for a quick hit of nostalgia.

Built on the back of AOSP builds for classic Nexus devices, “Android Time Machine” lets you rapidly access older Android versions. Specifically, Android 2.1 Eclair through Android 7.1.2 Nougat.

The simulator runs within the shell of a matching Nexus smartphone on a desktop browser, or to fit your actual smartphone if you run it on Android.

Versions and simulated smartphones include:.

The best part here is how it works on your actual smartphone. When launched in fullscreen, it scales to match your phone’s screen – meaning it fits even devices like the Galaxy Z Fold 8’s smaller outer display (it just shows the desktop version when open).

Since this is running through the browser and not an actual Android build, you won’t get a perfect replication. Performance is a little hit or miss, especially with certain animations, but it works really well overall.

The browser even simulates results from each era (oh, to go back to when Google Search wasn’t an absolute mess). Similarly, Google apps and the camera are filled with placeholders since the web app can’t access the actual camera or connect to the internet to sign into a Google account.

Seeing things like the boot animations and live wallpapers from classic Nexus phones, as well as peeking back at lost apps like Google+ and Play Music, is just such a fun little piece of nostalgia.

“Android Time Machine” is free, and the source code is available on GitHub.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A couple of years ago, Replit was flatlining at a few million dollars in annual revenue and running a mostly empty office after a layoff. Today the vibe coding pioneer is valued at $9 billion, up from $3 billion just six months ago. CEO Amjad Masad reveals what made the turnaround possible. Masad also weighs in on what he calls “AI psychosis,” and says cybersecurity, not AI extinction, is the risk worth focusing on. This is an abridged transcript of an interview from Rapid Response, recorded live at Masters of Scale Summit 2026 and hosted by former Fast Company editor-in-chief Robert Safian. From the team behind the Masters of Scale podcast, Rapid Response features candid conversations with today’s top business leaders navigating real-time challenges. Subscribe to Rapid Response wherever you get your podcasts to ensure you never miss an episode. The growth you’ve seen has been extraordinary. From the inside, what does that feel like? Is it exhilarating when everything is growing so fast? Is it terrifying? Do you have to pinch yourself to say, “Is this real?” It’s all of the above. The first feeling I had was a little bit of vindication, because I started talking about everyone being able to code and create software back in 2010, when I was building the kind of precursor to Replit as an open-source project. Then I was a founding engineer at Codecademy, where we taught a lot of people to code. And when we started Replit in 2016, we were like, “We want to blur this distinction between learning to code and doing code, and build an environment that really makes it so that anyone with an idea can build software.” And for a long time, people didn’t believe us. Raising capital was hard. Recruiting people was hard. Because some of the technology wasn’t ready yet. It wasn’t ready. It was on track, and I could see it happening. There were many moments where the company could have died, or I could have quit. It would have been very easy to quit at many different moments. And so in 2024, when we invented what would later be called vibe coding, when we came up with the first fully natural-language-based programming environment, there was nothing out there at the time. People really appreciated it, and we started seeing these stories of people having ideas. One of the early experiences I had was someone recording a video of themselves and posting it on Twitter and YouTube where they were crying because they had this idea of overlaying all their memories and their photos on a map and being able to explore their life through this map. It’s a simple idea, but it’s a personal app. It’s not even a commercial app. And he was crying because he said he had this idea for so long. He tried to do it with all these different technologies, and for the first time, he was able to do it. I’ve also been an angel investor for a while, and I’ve seen some early AI companies do the hypergrowth and the hyper-deceleration within a year. So there’s a fair amount of paranoia built into how we operate. You immigrated to the U.S. in 2012, and as you say, you spent years grinding away as you were trying to find your groove. Are there lessons from those slower times that you go back to as a leader in the midst of the noise you’re in now? Yeah. There were many moments where it felt darkest just before we were able to invent something big or newly introduced. Even just before we invented agentic coding in 2024, we had to do a layoff. We were six or seven years into the company, we had 2 or 3 million in ARR, and it was flatlining. It wasn’t growing at all. Two or three million? Yeah. Two or three million, just a couple of years ago. Now you’re at a billion. Yeah. I want to pause and acknowledge that. That’s crazy, man. It is wild. And we were burning a ton of money. We hired a great team, but the future hadn’t arrived as fast as I thought it would. So I kind of mistimed it a little bit. Unfortunately, we had to do a layoff. Around the same time, we also upgraded the office. We went from a small office in SF to this really massive office in Foster City because the space was so cheap there. It was this big office, but it felt dark and cold because it wasn’t really occupied. Every day, I would go into the office and sit at my desk and wait for another person to quit. The thing about doing a layoff is you also burst a bubble. You burst a dream. I’m sure a lot of people are familiar with Steve Jobs’s reality distortion field. Really, every founder needs to create some reality distortion. You’re selling a dream, and suddenly you’re saying, “We’re running out of money.” The dream immediately dissipates. I know you’re a believer that the idea of vibe coding is great, that everyone could be able to code. And you can code in natural language. I’m curious: Among your own team, you’ve got engineers who are building a product that essentially can make their job obsolete in some ways. There’s somewhat of an inherent tension inside the company, for sure. Some of our engineers are motivated by that. You’d be surprised. We have a few AI engineers who joined the team saying, “I want to automate my job.” It’s like, “What kind of motivation is that? Do you hate coding? Is that why?” But everyone inside is really excited by the impact we’re having on people’s lives, like the entrepreneurs we’re seeing build businesses that otherwise wouldn’t have been built because they suddenly have that power. That’s really what gets us excited. I do think we all face this question. Every knowledge worker essentially faces this question of, “The things that I’m doing might lead to my replacement,” because you’re generating data that is getting trained in the AI models, and that tension exists in tech broadly. In the tech neighborhood, you’ve decried what you call “AI psychosis.” You’ve called out Dario Amodei specifically at Anthropic for overheated predictions about AI-fed job losses. Today’s fear over AI agents run amok, is that also psychosis? Or is that a different AI risk? No. In fact, that is really the thing I’ve been talking about, the risk I’ve been talking about. I’ve been on the cybersecurity risk for two years now. I think everything else is a distraction from that. When they go out and talk about how AI is conscious, and they go meet the Pope and do all this random stuff, it’s really distracting, and it’s also, in many ways, destructive and bad for humanity for us to care about the well-being of these machines when we haven’t really figured out the well-being of humans. It also distracts from the real question of cybersecurity. Just in the past two or three days, we’ve had major platforms being hacked. And if you’re not paying attention, if you’re running an enterprise and you’re not paying attention to this stuff, if you’re running a company on some of these platforms that are insecure, you’re putting your business and your consumers at risk. I don’t think the world has taken that seriously. It’s a disaster brewing. The Hugging Face incident was the first kind of shot on that, but it’s not the end. This week has been pretty brutal for cybersecurity. Our team is working nonstop. Overnight, everyone’s in the office making sure we’re mitigating whatever vulnerabilities are coming up. It’s a very serious moment for the world, and the talk about AI extinction is just not relevant right now. We need to focus on cybersecurity.

#46774. Leaked Ohio bill could allow AI data center companies to seize private land for their buildouts using eminent domain law

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (518 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tomshardware ↗ Open Full Page

Leaked Ohio bill could allow AI data center companies to seize private land for their buildouts using eminent domain law

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (518 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that while Ohioans have rejected the building of latest data centers at every turn, they might not have much choice in the future.
  • In a recent development, legal experts have warned that the change could mean a transmission developer, like a power manufacturer, would be able to seize land to be used for a data center or a facility that would power one.
  • This follows a July 2026 report that the government was able to seize private land for upcoming transmission lines needed to power new data centers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that while Ohioans have rejected the building of latest data centers at every turn, they might not have much choice in the future. That's if a newly leaked bill that could allow data centers to be classified as public utilities is allowed to progress. The move would see the list of who can qualify for eminent domain law expanded, moving beyond entities owned or operated by municipal corporations, electric cooperatives, and agencies holding a certificate of public convenience and necessity granted by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission. The bill, leaked to WCPO Cincinnati, would add "and an agency holding a certificate of environmental compatibility and public need from the power siting board for constructing an electric transmission line and associated facilities or gas pipeline and its associated facilities.".

In a recent development, legal experts have warned that the change could mean a transmission developer, like a power manufacturer, would be able to seize land to be used for a data center or a facility that would power one. The writing has been on the wall for a while, too, after it was discovered in June that the Ohio Business Roundtable trade group recommended that lawmakers change eminent domain law to "extend possession authority to energy infrastructure projects once public use and necessity have been established.”.

This follows a July 2026 report that the government was able to seize private land for upcoming transmission lines needed to power new data centers. The law gives the government the power to take private land without the need for the owner's consent, so long as it is for public use and the owner receives appropriate compensation. The government can also delegate the same land-grabbing power to “private entities or common carriers,” which includes utility companies.

It has been revealed that this is already happening, too. Earlier this year, the largest utility manufacturer in Georgia required the removal of 30 residential properties in order to upgrade its grid. Residents claimed that the expansion was to power AI data centers, a fact given more weight by the fact that one such data center was located just a few miles away.

In a recent development, despite this, eminent domain law can still be used for good. Nashville set out to use the same law to block the building of a 69,220-square-foot single-story data center next to a zoo. Nashville Metro Council approved the use of eminent domain as a way to buy the land from a local developer who planned the $700 million data center buildout.
