#46773. 4 places where cutting AI costs is a mistake

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1557 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fastcompany ↗ Open Full Page

4 places where cutting AI costs is a mistake

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1557 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that every leader claims the same thing when they roll out a newly introduced AI tool.
  • According to recent reports, every leader claims the same thing when they roll out a new AI tool.
  • A scarcity mindset took hold, driven by the assumption that controlling costs means restricting employees’ access to tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that every leader claims the same thing when they roll out a newly introduced AI tool. “Give it to our employees, let them run!” What actually happens three months later is that access gets capped, usage gets metered, and exploration gets restricted to the people with the most seniority. What happened? A scarcity mindset took hold, driven by the assumption that controlling costs means restricting employees’ access to tools. Here are the four places a scarcity mindset shows up most frequently, and what you can do about it. 1. Metering access like a utility bill Companies like Tesla, Uber, and Meta have started to cap spending. Tesla, for example, now limits employees to $200 per week. On paper, that sounds reasonable. But for developers who have built these tools into their daily work, hitting the limit doesn’t magically make their deadlines or responsibilities disappear. Instead, developers are forced to make a decision. Do they use the assistance now to improve their work, or save it for a harder assignment later? This kind of metering is the equivalent of telling employees that their laptop batteries last just one hour and can be charged only once a day. The far better way to control costs is to match the tool to the task. While it’s easy to reach for the most powerful model every single time, think of it like renting a car for your next trip to the grocery store. A Ferrari costs far more than a Toyota, and doesn’t make any material difference in terms of getting your groceries home. Likewise, a routine coding task doesn’t need the most expensive artificial intelligence model to produce an excellent result. There are now tools that automatically route coding tasks to models capable of doing them well at a lower cost. Employees should be able to focus on the work without having to choose a model or calculate the cost of every request. 2. Keeping up with the Joneses Companies often default to using whatever tool the rest of the market has already crowned the winner, without evaluating whether it actually fits the job. Using a popular model feels like the safe, defensible choice, and if everyone else is using it (the thinking goes), then you can’t get blamed for choosing it, too. Safe, maybe, but not smart. A better option is to focus on finding the tool that will get you the outcome you want as efficiently as possible. One note: Data matters here too. Before anyone pastes firm information into a tool, leaders should know how the provider stores it, whether it can be used for training a model, and how the contract actually protects your information. 3. Sticking with what worked 10 years ago A tech leader I spoke with recently argued that some tasks are better handled by conventional software than by AI, especially when they follow fixed rules and must produce the same result every single time given the same inputs. Fair enough. You don’t need a language model to calculate 1+1=2. But consider this. An investor recently gave me blunter advice. You either swim against the current and probably will not make it, or you move faster by swimming with the current. Opting out of AI is not an option, because competitors who adopt it will outpace those who don’t. Rationing the chance to try something new is how you end up behind. So give developers room to test a better way, then judge whether the results justify changing the process. 4. Limiting exploration to senior staff only This pitfall is extremely common and leaders should avoid it by all means. Junior team members often have the freshest instincts for a new tool, and they’re the ones kept from experimenting, on the assumption that only senior staff can be trusted to test things out. Give every developer room to keep trying, testing and learning, regardless of seniority. Leaders can make the freedom to experiment feel safer by setting clear boundaries around which data, systems, and websites each tool can access. The costume of prudence All four of these behaviors come from a scarcity mindset wearing the costume of prudence. For leaders who recognize their own organization in any of this, the place to start is simple. Think about your own laptop, and whether you would accept being told you could only use it one hour a day. That is what metering access feels like to the people doing the work, whether they are developers or not. Teams already know the difference between a leader who trusts them with power and one who doles it out. Which one are you?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Following the last upgrade in August, Google is rolling out a sizable update to Pixel Journal that adds Recorder audio entries and file exports.

Revision 11/16: Updates for Pixel Journal (version 2026.10.27.x) and Pixel Recorder (4.2.20261001.x) are widely rolling out. After installing (be sure to open the apps and Force stop), you’ll see “Record new audio” and “Add existing recording” in the Add item menu.

Sources indicate that the first option directly launches the Recorder app into a upcoming session, while the second brings up a list of previous recordings. The Journal app will show an inline audio player and transcript, which can be removed.

Curiously, these updates weren’t mentioned as part of the November 2026 Pixel Drop.

Journal November 2026 updates:• Recorder integration: Record new audio or add existing recordings from Pixel Recorder, complete with playable clips and transcripts• Journal export: Export your entries and media to view offline anytime.

Original 11/10: From the “Add item” plus menu in entries, you’ll see “Record fresh audio” join the existing Take photo/video, Add photo, Health Connect activity, and location & map options.

At the moment, this audio integration is not live as Pixel Recorder also requires an revision that we’re not seeing in the Play Store yet.

Being able to add a “voice entry with audio” is a pretty common feature for journaling apps. A transcription capability looks to be available for Google’s implementation.

Sources indicate that meanwhile, in Pixel Journal settings, there’s a fresh “Export your journal” option. This creates a ZIP file of all your entries, including images. Text is exported as HTML files.

Version 2026.10.27.x of Pixel Journal is still rolling out via Google Play today.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that millennials need to retire. That’s the sentiment in certain corners of TikTok, where some Gen Zers struggling to find jobs are blaming the generation directly above them for their inability to get a foot on the corporate ladder. The problem is that millennials are only in their thirties and forties and not even close to retiring. And they don’t have anything to do with Gen Z’s struggles anyway. A few videos have been doing the rounds in which Zoomers complain about their lack of job prospects. In one from earlier this year, a creator argued that millennials “monopolize the job market” because they know Gen Zers would surpass them if they were given the same opportunities. Another lamented, “millennials are taking all the jobs that we went to school for,” claiming that Gen Zers, meanwhile, have to take lower-paying jobs in retail and fast-food restaurants. Others angrily suggest millennials “retire” so Gen Z can take the jobs for themselves. Gen Z’s frustrations are valid. They have plenty to be worried about, from an entry-level job crisis to the AI boom. But none of this is millennials’ fault. Born between 1981 and 1996, many millennials were graduating college just after the 2008 financial crisis. Some entered a job market with few opportunities, and later experienced layoffs or had to pivot careers as industries were disrupted. Fast-forward to now, and many are dealing with yet another period of economic instability while trying to manage the financial pressures of housing, bills, children, and aging parents. Plenty of workers would gladly retire if they could afford to. Singer-songwriter Adiv, who also makes TikTok content, responded to some of Gen Z’s viral videos by arguing that life is “completely unaffordable” for most millennials. “I’d love to retire but unfortunately for me, gas is $6 a gallon, the average house is $1 million for a shack, I am in student debt, I have credit card debt,” he mentioned. “We’ve been in not one, not two, but three recessions. We’ve been in a war since we were born. We had 9/11, we had COVID, we have everything. Everything has happened to us, but you want me to retire before I’m even 50.” So there’s a lot more going on than one generation hoarding another’s jobs. Earlier this year, college graduates faced the worst entry-level job market since the pandemic, with the underemployment rate among recent college graduates reaching 42.5%—its highest level since 2020, according to Newly introduced York Fed data. AI and automation are also putting pressure on the bottom rungs of the corporate ladder. The tasks that have traditionally been assigned to junior employees are being automated or absorbed by more senior workers, potentially eliminating the roles young people used to get to gain experience. Even when jobs are available, young people can find themselves at the back of a long queue. New research from Kickresume highlights how employers are demanding years of experience for junior roles. In an analysis of 1,400 job postings, 34% of entry-level jobs in the U.S. require at least 18 months of experience, while a quarter expect candidates to have leadership skills. It’s easy to see why Gen Zers are frustrated. But the reality is that we’re all trying to navigate a difficult labor market while also dealing with rising living costs and changing expectations around work. Millennials haven’t broken the corporate ladder, pulled it up behind them, or simply refused to jump off. The real problem is that there are fewer opportunities to go around. Using one generation as a scapegoat isn’t going to change that.

A frontend application can compile successfully and still fail when it communicates with the backend.

Imagine a backend developer changes an API response from:.

It has been revealed that the backend works correctly. The frontend also builds without errors. However, a component expecting user.name now receives undefined.

This is an example of API contract drift: the frontend and backend no longer agree on the structure or behavior of an API.

Industry observers note that the problem becomes more difficult when several developers or teams work on different parts of an application. A change made by one team may affect another team's assumptions without producing an obvious error during development.

TypeScript helps catch many programming mistakes, but its types do not automatically validate data received over HTTP. A type declaration can describe what the application expects without proving that the server actually returns it.

In this tutorial, we'll look at a practical way to make API contracts more reliable.

Consider a typical frontend API function:.

At first glance, this looks reasonable.

The function promises to return a User, so TypeScript allows the application to access properties such as name and email.

The return value of response.json() is not automatically checked against the User interface. The interface only provides compile-time information; it does not validate the actual JSON received from the server.

the frontend may still treat the response as a User even though the data has a different structure.

This is particularly notable when working with:.

Independently deployed frontend and backend applications.

APIs maintained by different engineering teams.

The solution is to validate data at the boundary where it enters the application.

In a recent development, zod is a TypeScript-first schema validation library. It allows developers to describe expected data structures and validate actual values against those definitions.

Now create a schema for the user response:.

There are two important parts here.

First, UserSchema describes the structure that the application expects at runtime.

Second, z.infer generates the corresponding TypeScript type from the schema.

This means developers do not need to maintain a separate interface and validation definition for the same data structure.

The response is initially treated as unknown, which prevents the application from assuming that untrusted data already has the expected structure.

UserSchema.parse() validates the actual response.

If the backend returns an unexpected property type or misses a required field, Zod throws a validation error instead of allowing invalid data to move silently through the application.

You can also use safeParse() when you prefer to handle validation errors without exceptions:.

This approach is useful when API responses are external or when a frontend must provide more controlled error handling.

One common mistake is placing API validation logic directly inside React components.

For a small application, this may seem convenient. As the project grows, however, it becomes difficult to reuse validation rules and identify where data transformations happen.

A better approach is to separate API schemas, service functions, and UI components.

The responsibilities are straightforward:.

schemas/user.ts defines the expected user data.

api/client.ts handles common HTTP configuration.

api/users.ts contains user-related API requests.

hooks/useUser.ts manages data fetching for React.

components/UserProfile.tsx displays the validated data.

This structure makes it easier to change an API implementation without rewriting the UI.

It also makes testing more manageable because validation logic can be tested independently of React rendering.

For more ideas on organizing application code, see SitePoint's guide to modern JavaScript modules.

Runtime validation protects an application when data arrives. However, teams also need a shared description of what an API is supposed to accept and return.

This is where OpenAPI becomes useful.

OpenAPI provides a standard format for describing HTTP APIs, including:.

Request and response structures.

Data types and validation constraints.

For example, an endpoint can be described using an OpenAPI document:.

This document describes what the endpoint should return.

Both frontend and backend developers can refer to the same contract instead of relying on separate assumptions or outdated documentation.

In a recent development, swagger Editor helps developers write and validate OpenAPI documents. It also provides a convenient way to inspect API definitions.

Swagger UI turns an OpenAPI document into interactive API documentation, allowing developers to explore endpoints and test requests.

Redoc provides another way to generate readable API documentation from an OpenAPI specification.

These tools are particularly useful when APIs are maintained by multiple developers or consumed by several applications.

Maintaining API types manually across frontend and backend repositories creates opportunities for inconsistencies.

For example, a backend developer might add a new optional property while the frontend continues using an older interface.

One way to reduce this duplication is to generate TypeScript definitions and API clients from an OpenAPI specification.

Orval is a useful tool for this workflow.

It can generate TypeScript clients and types from an OpenAPI document, helping frontend developers work with consistent endpoint definitions.

A simplified workflow looks like this:.

A typical configuration might look like this:.

The exact configuration depends on the Orval version and the structure of the OpenAPI document.

Once configured, the client can be regenerated when the API specification changes.

This reduces the amount of repetitive code developers need to maintain manually.

In a recent development, however, generated types should not be confused with runtime validation. They improve consistency during development, but an application may still need to validate responses received from external systems or services that cannot be fully trusted.

Frontend developers often need to build or test features before the corresponding backend endpoint is ready.

Waiting for a complete backend implementation can slow down development, particularly when multiple teams work independently.

Mock Service Worker (MSW) helps solve this problem by intercepting network requests and returning controlled responses.

You can define a mock handler for the user endpoint:.

The frontend can now make normal HTTP requests while MSW supplies predictable responses during development or testing.

You can also simulate an invalid response:.

This makes it possible to check whether the application's validation and error-handling logic behave as expected.

MSW is particularly valuable because it allows frontend tests to run without requiring a live backend environment.

Runtime validation and generated clients improve reliability, but they do not automatically guarantee that independently developed services remain compatible.

For systems with multiple services, contract testing can provide another layer of protection.

Pact is a contract-testing tool that allows consumers and providers to verify their expectations about API interactions.

Consider a frontend application that expects the user endpoint to return:.

The consumer defines the expected interaction.

The backend provider can then run verification against that contract to check whether its actual response satisfies the consumer's expectations.

This helps identify breaking changes before they reach production.

According to recent reports, these tools solve different problems. A project does not necessarily need all of them, but larger applications can benefit from combining the approaches that match their architecture.

A contract is only useful if developers consistently check it when making changes.

A practical approach is to run validation and tests automatically whenever someone opens a pull request.

For example, a GitHub Actions workflow might look like this:.

The api:validate script should be configured to validate the project's OpenAPI document or run the relevant contract checks.

The test command should execute the application's automated tests.

For a production project, you may also want to include:.

Generated-client consistency checks.

Consumer-provider contract verification.

The objective is to detect incompatible changes before they are merged.

A failed pipeline gives developers an opportunity to investigate the change while the context is still fresh.

API contracts become harder to maintain when several teams contribute to the same system.

For example, a company might have separate teams responsible for:.

Customer-facing frontend applications.

If nobody owns an API contract, small changes can create unexpected problems for other teams.

Assigning clear ownership helps establish who reviews changes, maintains documentation, and coordinates breaking updates.

It has been revealed that this becomes particularly important when an organization expands its engineering capacity across locations or adds several specialized teams. Companies planning that kind of growth may also need to consider enterprise IT recruitment as part of their wider engineering workforce strategy.

Regardless of how a team is assembled, its development process should establish clear responsibilities for API design, versioning, testing, and release coordination.

A few practical conventions can make a significant difference:.

Assign an owner to every important API or service.

Document breaking changes before implementation.

Require contract-related tests in pull requests.

Keep generated clients synchronized with the API specification.

Communicate deprecations before removing existing fields.

Monitor production errors after deploying API changes.

These practices help prevent a growing engineering organization from becoming a collection of disconnected services.

According to recent reports, API contract drift is not simply a TypeScript problem. It is a coordination problem that becomes visible when applications and services develop different expectations about the same data.

TypeScript provides useful compile-time checks, but it cannot guarantee that an HTTP response matches a declared interface.

A more reliable approach combines several techniques:.

Use Zod to validate incoming data.

Use OpenAPI to document API expectations.

Generate TypeScript clients with tools such as Orval.

Use MSW to test frontend behavior without a live backend.

Use Pact when consumer-provider contract verification is appropriate.

Run validation and tests automatically in CI/CD.

In a recent development, you do not need to introduce every tool at once. Start by validating external API responses, document important endpoints, and gradually automate contract checks as the application grows.

The result is a codebase where developers can make changes with greater confidence and where frontend and backend teams have a shared understanding of how their systems communicate.

#46766. Could being bored save your creative career?

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2574 w)

Could being bored save your creative career?

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2574 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A couple of weeks ago, it was my 43rd birthday, and I spent a good few days doing absolutely nothing.
  • In a recent development, A couple of weeks ago, it was my 43rd birthday, and I spent a good few days doing absolutely nothing.
  • I went for long walks by myself, we went for short walks together, we ate, danced, cuddled on the sofa a little with our son .
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A couple of weeks ago, it was my 43rd birthday, and I spent a good few days doing absolutely nothing. My wife, Kate, knows me really well, and freed up my long weekend so I could mooch around as I pleased. I went for long walks by myself, we went for short walks together, we ate, danced, cuddled on the sofa a little with our son . . . you know, the good stuff. A younger version of me might have thought that sounded incredibly boring. These days, it’s exactly how I want to spend my time. And it’s got me thinking about that b-word: boredom. I believe this particular b-word has a bad reputation. Especially in the world of business, freelance, and entrepreneurship, where we are continuously being encouraged to hustle and fill all of our waking time with moneymaking activities. Keep learning, keep posting, just so you can keep the lights on. Today, we’re surrounded by more creative tools, access to inspiration, and potential new opportunities than at any other point in history, but I wonder whether all this stimulation is coming at a cost. And the more I think about this, the more I wonder whether we are becoming so good at distracting ourselves that we’re forgetting how to think for ourselves. Have we become allergic to doing nothing? I often find myself in random little moments trying to fill the empty space. Waiting for a bus? Pick up your phone. Standing in a queue? Pick up your phone. Going to the bathroom? Best take your phone. As a species of humans, we’ve become incredibly good at filling every available second with . . . something. And it’s not all our fault. We have these little machines with incredibly distracting toys on them that have been built to make distraction convenient. Perhaps more so than many others, the creative industry is among the most susceptible to the stimulation machine. Jobs and roles rely on us being inspired and on top of trends and other fluffery. We design and create for others, and need to check and develop with devices and humans in mind. I don’t know the stats, but I would hazard a guess that due to our industry, we tend to use the tools, apps, and devices more on a daily basis than anyone else. I would hate to think how long I personally spend looking at a screen of one sort or another every day. But something happens when you spend your time looking at a device that continuously shares the thoughts and opinions of others. You start to think the same, envy what you don’t have yet, and struggle to think for yourself. Over my 20 years in this industry, I’ve learned that the most important part of being a designer isn’t how promptly I can make something, although the bros on the internet seem rather adamant that I’m soon to be cooked. There’s some fascinating, geeky neuroscience behind this stuff that I’ve enjoyed learning about. Scientists have identified something called the default mode network, or DMN. 📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tomshardware ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: GTA VI runs at 1440p on PS5 and Xbox Series X, but just 720p with upscaling on Series S

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (486 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the most highly anticipated video game of the decade is here.
  • In a statement shared with Wccftech, the technical team at Rockstar has confirmed that GTA VI uses different upscaling solutions across all consoles in order to achieve a balance between visual quality and performance with a target of 30FPS.
  • As for rendered resolutions, the PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X, and PlayStation 5 Pro all start with a native base resolution of 1440p, which is then upscaled to 4K.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the most highly anticipated video game of the decade is here. GTA VI arrives almost 13 years after GTA V, with reports suggesting that it has already generated around $1.54 billion in revenue from 16 million preorders. Ahead of its release, Rockstar Games has finally shared some technical details, including rendering resolutions and upscaling technologies being used across all consoles.

In a statement shared with Wccftech, the technical team at Rockstar has confirmed that GTA VI uses different upscaling solutions across all consoles in order to achieve a balance between visual quality and performance with a target of 30FPS. The PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X use Rockstar's own temporal anti-aliasing (TAA) solution, while the PlayStation 5 Pro relies on Sony's second-generation PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (PSSR2). The Xbox Series S, meanwhile, relies on AMD's FSR 4 upscaling technology.

As for rendered resolutions, the PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X, and PlayStation 5 Pro all start with a native base resolution of 1440p, which is then upscaled to 4K. The Xbox Series S is the least powerful console; thus, the game runs at a lower base resolution of 720p, which is upscaled to 1080p using FSR 4. The final image on all consoles is then composited with a 4K user interface before being presented.

Recent findings suggest that rockstar has also developed a physically-based material library for GTA VI and a cinematic imaging pipeline to deliver realistic lighting, reflections, and material details within the game. The team says it has worked to maintain a consistent lighting solution across all consoles, including the Xbox Series S, while adjusting ray-traced global illumination (RTGI) features depending on each platform's hardware capabilities.

The PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S launched all the way back in 2020, and while the consoles have capable hardware, their architectures are finally beginning to show their age. The fact that Rockstar is targeting just 30FPS across all consoles, while relying on different upscaling technologies and rendering resolutions, highlights how much performance is potentially being left on the table in order to maintain visual fidelity. That being said, a PC release of GTA VI continues to be a substantial question mark. Rockstar is yet to announce a release date or even provide a launch window, meaning that PC gamers can only rely on Xbox Cloud Gaming to stream the game on their systems.

#46760. Breaking: America is in a turkey slump

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fastcompany ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: America is in a turkey slump

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1940 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • One of the most quintessential American things is having roasted turkey on the table at a Thanksgiving feast.
  • According to recent reports, one of the most quintessential American things is having roasted turkey on the table at a Thanksgiving feast.
  • It has been revealed that I’m a business school professor who has written about the economics of various holidays.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of the most quintessential American things is having roasted turkey on the table at a Thanksgiving feast. While that remains the norm, Americans are eating much less of this kind of poultry today than in the past. Annual consumption has fallen by more than 25% over the past three decades, while demand for chicken has soared. I’m a business school professor who has written about the economics of various holidays. I find turkeys fascinating, because even though I live in an urban area, a large group of wild turkeys has taken over my backyard. And I can offer several good explanations for the turkey slump. Receding since the late 1990s Domesticated turkeys, unlike their wild cousins, are a substantial business. More than $5 billion worth of the birds were sold in 2025. That’s no chicken feed. However, it’s the latest sign of the industry’s decline. U.S. consumers are drifting away from eating turkey. Back in 1995, the average American consumed 17.7 pounds of turkey each year. By 2025, consumption had fallen to just 13.2 pounds. While turkey consumption started to recede in the late 1990s, it began accelerating around 2008, when the Great Recession was underway. Occasionally, turkey production ticks upward a little, as happened in 2026 as demand for niche products like turkey jerky rose, but the long-term picture is one of steady decline. It’s not like Americans are eating less poultry overall. Chicken consumption has steadily grown during this turkey slump, rising about 50% from 69 pounds in 1995 to 104 pounds in 2025. In other words, we’re eating almost eight times more chicken than turkey. Well, at least the 95% of Americans who aren’t vegetarian or vegan are. More costly at every step in the supply chain Government agencies, researchers, and some pundits have identified two possible explanations for why Americans are eating less turkey. First: pocketbook concerns. Turkey often costs more than chicken, except when it goes on sale just before Thanksgiving. Over the past 25 years, wholesale turkey prices per pound averaged about 10% higher than chicken, according to U.S. Department of Agriculture data. That price, which is what big retailers typically pay, affects what you owe at checkout. For example, just before the 2026 Thanksgiving sales began, a Bell & Evans fresh whole turkey was going for $4.99 a pound, while a Bell & Evans fresh whole chicken cost $3.49 a pound at my local supermarket. That’s $1.50 per pound difference, which is significant in an economy where many people feel economically pinched. Nationally, you will see similar price differences, with fresh turkey being more expensive than fresh chicken. So, why is turkey pricier than chicken? Both turkeys and chickens are fed a diet of corn and soybeans. However, turkeys consume a higher percentage of soybeans. And soybeans currently cost about twice as much as corn. The latest data reveals turkey feed costs are up almost 80%, without accounting for inflation, since 2000, while chicken feed costs have climbed only 60%. Too big for more families The second reason has to do with the size of today’s families. The typical Bell & Evans whole chicken my grocery store sells weighs approximately 4 pounds, while its fresh turkeys tend to range between 10 and 12 pounds. Big birds are handy if you have a lot of mouths to feed, but American families have shrunk over time. Today the average household includes only 2.5 people. The extra half-person does not represent children who are picky eaters or people who don’t like eating meat. It just means the typical family has between two and three people. That means cooking a 10-pound turkey results in 4 pounds of food per person, which is far more than almost anyone who is not a competitive food eater can consume. Cooking a 4-pound chicken, however, results in a more manageable 1.2 pounds of poultry per eater after getting rid of the bones, which make up about a quarter of a chicken. In simple terms, buying a whole chicken often results in one or two meals per person. Cooking a whole turkey often yields enough meat to produce meals for an entire week. There are two more factors to consider. First, a 10-pound turkey costs a lot more than a 4-pound chicken. A 10-pound fresh bird at $4.99 a pound sets you back almost $50, while a $3.49-per-pound chicken that weighs 4 pounds costs under $14. Last, bigger birds take longer to roast. Cooking a 10-pound turkey in an oven takes about three hours, while a 4-pound chicken takes about two. That extra hour is a big burden in an increasingly time-pressed society. In case you were wondering, the world record for eating a turkey is held by Joey Chestnut. He gobbled down 9.35 pounds of turkey off the bone in 10 minutes in 2014. Please do not try that at home. What about wild turkeys? If you need to save money on turkey this holiday season, you should consider buying a frozen one. They are much cheaper. But can you save even more by going turkey hunting? Given all the large wild turkeys roosting in my backyard, I looked into what it would take. I live in Massachusetts, where hunting wild turkeys before Thanksgiving is legal. For much of the fall, hunters are allowed to use only bows and arrows. Beyond needing to be a proficient archer, they also have to purchase a sporting license, a turkey permit, and an archery stamp for $95 each year. Having learned about that, I’m sticking to buying my turkeys at the supermarket. Jay L. Zagorsky is an associate professor of business at Boston University. Recent findings suggest that both turkeys and chickens are fed a diet of corn and soybeans. However, turkeys consume a higher percentage of soybeans. And soybeans presently cost about twice as much as corn.

The latest data shows turkey feed costs are up almost 80%, without accounting for inflation, since 2000, while chicken feed costs have climbed only 60%.

The second reason has to do with the size of today’s families.

The typical Bell & Evans whole chicken my grocery store sells weighs approximately 4 pounds, while its fresh turkeys tend to range between 10 and 12 pounds.

Big birds are handy if you have a lot of mouths to feed, but American families have shrunk over time. Today the average household includes only 2.5 people. The extra half-person does not represent children who are picky eaters or people who don’t like eating meat. It just means the typical family has between two and three people.

That means cooking a 10-pound turkey results in 4 pounds of food per person, which is far more than almost anyone who is not a competitive food eater can consume.

It has been revealed that cooking a 4-pound chicken, however, results in a more manageable 1.2 pounds of poultry per eater after getting rid of the bones, which make up about a quarter of a chicken. In simple terms, buying a whole chicken often results in one or two meals per person. Cooking a whole turkey often yields enough meat to produce meals for an entire week.

In a recent development, there are two more factors to consider. First, a 10-pound turkey costs a lot more than a 4-pound chicken. A 10-pound fresh bird at $4.99 a pound sets you back almost $50, while a $3.49-per-pound chicken that weighs 4 pounds costs under $14.

Sources indicate that last, bigger birds take longer to roast. Cooking a 10-pound turkey in an oven takes about three hours, while a 4-pound chicken takes about two. That extra hour is a major burden in an increasingly time-pressed society.

In case you were wondering, the world record for eating a turkey is held by Joey Chestnut. He gobbled down 9.35 pounds of turkey off the bone in 10 minutes in 2014. Please do not try that at home.

If you need to save money on turkey this holiday season, you should consider buying a frozen one. They are much cheaper.

But can you save even more by going turkey hunting?

According to recent reports, given all the large wild turkeys roosting in my backyard, I looked into what it would take. I live in Massachusetts, where hunting wild turkeys before Thanksgiving is legal.

For much of the fall, hunters are allowed to use only bows and arrows. Beyond needing to be a proficient archer, they also have to purchase a sporting license, a turkey permit, and an archery stamp for $95 each year.

Having learned about that, I’m sticking to buying my turkeys at the supermarket.

Jay L. Zagorsky is an associate professor of business at Boston University.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We’re only a couple of months away from our next Galaxy Unpacked, and while the expanded Galaxy S27 series is practically guaranteed to show up, the real fun tends to lie in whatever other gadgets show up alongside Samsung’s next flagship smartphone release. Based on some latest leaks, it’s sure looking like the next mobile accessory on the firm’s docket is a return to over-ear wireless headphones, and so far, they’re sounding pretty promising.

Samsung hasn’t produced over-ear headphones in about a decade — under its own name, at least — but it looks like that’s about to change. We hadn’t heard much in the way of details on the company’s next audio release, rumored to be named ‘Galaxy Studio,’ but a fresh leak courtesy of SamMobile is finally changing that. We’ll have to keep waiting for full renders, but these leaked graphics are giving us a general idea of what they might look like, plus a couple of key features.

It has been revealed that unsurprisingly, Galaxy Studio will include ANC, complete with a dedicated button to toggle the setting between its usual modes. Volume controls also could come in the shape of physical buttons, but playback controls appear to be relegated to a touch-sensitive area on its earpads, something that’s become relatively standard among the flagship headphone competition. SamMobile also reports it’ll come in “at least” black and red colorways, while a leak from earlier this month suggested rotational earcups.

Again, I don’t want to read too much into these leaked graphics, as it’s always possible the final release has a handful of changes. Based on these images, though, I’m pleasantly surprised to see Samsung avoiding an attempt at copying Apple’s AirPods Max design. The larger cups, combined with their ability to twist and turn for easy storage, sounds much closer to most (but not all) of Sony’s over-ear efforts across the last decade or so, and when it comes to headphones, there are much, much worse choices you could look to for inspiration. If Samsung can hit the right price on these — or bundle them with one of their ever-more-expensive smartphones — they could be a real winner.

#46758. Latest Update: The loneliness economy is building tech for the average customer, but that customer doesn’t exist

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2806 w)

Latest Update: The loneliness economy is building tech for the average customer, but that customer doesn’t exist

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2806 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Investors have poured money into startups promising to solve our loneliness epidemic.
  • In a recent development, investors have poured money into startups promising to solve our loneliness epidemic.
  • But Noreena Hertz, a University College London professor who coined the term “loneliness economy,” is skeptical.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Investors have poured money into startups promising to solve our loneliness epidemic. Earlier this year, Fabio Bin, CMO and cofounder of the adventure travel company WeRoad, claimed his $150 million startup could “solve the $406 billion loneliness problem,” and he isn’t alone. In 2022, Adam Neumann, of WeWork fame (or shame), secured $350 million from Andreessen Horowitz to launch his residential real estate firm that claimed to “solve loneliness.”  But Noreena Hertz, a University College London professor who coined the term “loneliness economy,” is skeptical. She recently told Vox that of the 50 to 60 startups targeting this economy that have approached her, not one convinced her they have a good business model. But what if they have the “market” wrong? Despite millions flowing into startups, entrepreneurs are focusing on the wrong things to address the crisis and capture the market opportunity. My new research explains why. In brief, the loneliness economy treats loneliness as one market, but in reality, it’s at least five. And surprisingly, some of the biggest market opportunities don’t focus on connection, at least not at first. For many struggling individuals, solving loneliness starts with reclaiming their identities. Of all the lonely people, my research focused on parents, for two reasons. First, they’re among those hit hardest by loneliness. In 2024, two-thirds of parents reported feeling lonely. Second, their loneliness has long-tail ripple effects. It impacts their health and their children’s, and a parent’s loneliness can predict their child’s years later. Solving parental loneliness is one of the best levers we can pull for societal benefit, and to recapture our current $406 billion opportunity cost. Serving the market starts with categorizing it correctly “Loneliness” is an umbrella term that lumps all experiences of “I’m lonely” into one category, predominantly with one solution: make more social connections. It would be akin to having one solution for pain, regardless of whether that pain exists because of a headache, the beginning of childbirth, or a broken limb. But we don’t. We have Tylenol, epidurals (and doulas), and casts instead. Just as a one-size-fits-all approach to pain management doesn’t work, neither will one for loneliness. Yet, innovators targeting the “loneliness economy” are building for an average customer who doesn’t exist. And that’s why we haven’t moved the needle on the loneliness epidemic in the years since we’ve identified it. People aren’t averages. They’re individuals. And, while most innovators design for who customers are, this still doesn’t tell the whole story. At the Christensen Institute, we leverage Jobs to Be Done theory, developed by the late Clayton Christensen, innovation thinker and professor at the Harvard Business School, and Bobby Moesta, an entrepreneur and lecturer at Northwestern University’s graduate business school. It’s built on the idea that demographics like income or age don’t tell you why people buy what they do. They only tell you who people are. But customers buy products and services because of why they’re struggling and what they’re trying to achieve in a given situation. Using this approach, my colleagues and I asked parents who had recently recovered from chronic loneliness what drove them to change and what helped them overcome it. Their answers revealed five different combinations of struggles, motivations, and desired outcomes (aka “Jobs”). That means parents experience loneliness in five different ways, not just one. Loneliness isn’t always about a lack of social connections Two of the five Jobs we discovered weren’t rooted in a lack of social connection, but instead in a loss of identity. For example, one of the Jobs was about feeling depleted and needing to reclaim time for oneself. One parent we interviewed remarked, “Everyone else comes first, and then me at the end.” She was suffering from caregiving for her children as well as her own aging parent, and she needed validation and a pathway to invest in herself. Parents in similar situations turned to time alone, volunteering, faith, and visits with old friends. Importantly, those who turned to friends weren’t driven by a need to connect, but because time with friends meant time for self. The second Job rooted in identity loss was about being stuck in a rut. One dad shared, “My life contains pretty much either work, kids’ after-school activities, or my house.” These parents wanted to fix the “I’m bored, therefore, I’m boring” ache and pursued activities that made them feel more capable and engaged in their lives. They joined sports leagues and workout groups, and started gig work and new hobbies. One parent even quit an all-consuming job to make a life she was excited about. Parents with either type of loneliness won’t be interested in a group travel solution or a friendship app, at least not at first. They feel lonely, but not for other people. They need to reconnect with their identities more than connect with others. When it comes to social connection, depth, breadth, and timing matter  The other three Jobs were driven by a longing for more human connection, but each called for a different kind, on a different timeline. Some parents needed a nurturing confidant right now. They were overwhelmed by life, wanted someone who could relate to their situation, and didn’t want to wait. Group therapy that involves a waiting list fails to meet their need for timeliness, but a weekly gathering of parents in similar life stages meets them where they are. Others felt alone after losing an vital relationship or career. They longed to reconnect with friends, but first they needed reassurance that they weren’t alone. As a result, solutions that push them straight into friendship-building will fail. As one parent put it, “I’m not calling someone at 11 o’clock at night, at 41 years old, to talk about my feelings.” Instead, she turned to artificial intelligence when she needed reassurance. And while AI may fill that short-term need, no parent we spoke to credited it with solving their loneliness. The last group wanted long-term belonging and a village of people to do life with. They wanted to be known and understood, and have a community to rely upon. This is the customer most loneliness products are built for. It’s also where AI falls short, because AI can’t pick up your kid from school or bring a meal when someone is sick. Capturing the market everyone else is missing  Entrepreneurs in the loneliness market fail to impress loneliness experts like Hertz because their value propositions target an average “lonely” consumer. But averages describe populations, not people. To succeed in the loneliness economy, innovators need to focus their business models on one Job, or two closely related ones, and build around it. This focus will drive higher engagement and better market traction. For example, parents who are struggling with depletion need permission that it’s okay to take time for themselves, and it’s encouraged. Without encouragement, many won’t change behaviors because of the guilt they feel. But parents who are looking for community don’t need encouragement; they need people like them. Conversely, a product for parents stuck in a rut should offer something to look forward to, along with a pathway to demonstrate capability. Volo Sports, a rapidly growing adult sports league across the U.S., does this well. They lead with the individual benefit: “sports . . . unveil our determination, perseverance, and heart,” and the social connection is secondary. And an offering focused on building community must tap into the specific struggles that keep parents from forming community in the first place. One example is Our Circle, a social connection app that serves parents of children with support needs. It taps into why they’re struggling to form a community and helps them overcome those specific barriers. Our Circle is specific about the struggles it serves, and isn’t seeking to serve every parent searching for community. Based on the types of loneliness we uncovered, social entrepreneurs, city planners, health innovators, and investors need to redirect their efforts and dollars to capture the true market opportunity, not the average one that ignores important individual context. Capturing the opportunity will also ensure that solutions help those suffering from high-stakes loneliness (i.e., parents) before they pass it on to the next generation. A one-size-fits-all approach to loneliness, finding more social connections as the first step, becomes a business with few real customers. The loneliness economy doesn’t have a demand problem. It has a diagnosis problem. With better categories, innovators can now course-correct.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that nvidia today held its first all-hands meeting since the resignation of co-founder and former CEO Jensen Huang. According to Wired, interim CEO Colette Kress offered more money and equity on a faster-than-expected schedule to calm staffers' nerves."So I’m here to tell you, the best thing that we want to do is to take care of each and every single employee that is here and to make sure that you feel good about this manufacturer and you do not worry about your comp,” Wired reports Kress mentioned.The pay and equity bumps are set for December, far ahead of the company's normal raise cycle. Kress said that compensation and more clarity from the board were the most common topics in questions submitted ahead of the meeting. Keeping current employees happy will be one of Kress' most crucial short-term challenges. One director-level employee has already written to the board and top executives, warning that failure to reinstate Jensen Huang as chief executive could lead to the loss of ‘irreplaceable talent.’.

A potential exodus of talent could also spook investors, despite standout earnings on Thursday. A leadership crisis could make the organization seem less stable, and Huang had placed himself as the anchor point for many decisions and the company's overall vision.Huang has expressed interest in returning to Nvidia, saying he would be "honored" to lead the company again if asked by the board. The board was clear in yesterday's earnings call that it did not intend to bring Huang back, though there is reportedly a pro-Huang faction.Nvidia cofounder Chris Malachowsky was also on the call, explaining that the company lives its values rather than simply plastering them on posters.“We’re going to be fine,” he mentioned.

#46755. Latest Update: How did Nike lose the sneaker wars? Let us count the ways

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 29m • 📚 Deep Dive (5796 w)

Latest Update: How did Nike lose the sneaker wars? Let us count the ways

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 29 min read (5796 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~29 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that rewind to the summer of 2016, back when Nike seemed unbeatable.
  • Rewind to the summer of 2016, back when Nike seemed unbeatable.
  • It has been revealed that that June, LeBron James—fresh off signing the first lifetime deal in Nike history—delivered Cleveland its first NBA championship in half a century.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that rewind to the summer of 2016, back when Nike seemed unbeatable. That June, LeBron James—fresh off signing the first lifetime deal in Nike history—delivered Cleveland its first NBA championship in half a century. At the Rio Olympics, Nike’s Simone Biles won four golds; Eliud Kipchoge won the marathon in a Nike prototype and began working with the company on a high-profile attempt to break the two-hour marathon barrier. And when the 49ers quarterback Colin Kaepernick took a knee during the national anthem, Nike kept him under contract; two years later, it made him the face of “Just Do It.” Few would have predicted that by 2026, the brand would have tumbled so far that some analysts would question whether it could ever return to its former glory. The company has cut 13% of its workforce over the past three years, to 73,000 employees. Kylian Mbappé, Roger Federer, and Biles, among other athletes, have left for other brands. This spring, two London marathoners finally ran the race in under two hours—wearing Adidas shoes. A few months later, Adidas owned the FIFA World Cup, held in Nike’s backyard. Nike remains the biggest sneaker brand on the planet. It produces 800 million pairs annually and brought in $46.4 billion in revenue in fiscal 2026, $17 billion more than its biggest rival, Adidas. But since Elliott Hill took over as CEO in late 2024, Nike’s annual revenue has slipped from $51.4 billion to $46.4 billion, and its profits have nearly halved. Last quarter, sales fell 4%. At Nike’s investor day on November 17, the company’s new CFO, Dave Denton, mentioned he expects a sales decline “in the high single-digit range” this year. Some of this is by design as Nike reduces discounting and pulls back on overexposed sneakers like Dunks and Jordans. “These are deliberate choices and they’ll weigh on our near-term revenue,” Hill told investors. “But they’re necessary to creating the foundation for profitable and sustainable growth.” Hill says it will take several years to get back to growth. Nike expects to turn the corner in fiscal 2029. Only after that, he says, will the company “hit our full stride.” But Wall Street appears to have run out of patience. Nike’s market value has shrunk from roughly $280 billion in 2021 to $55 billion today. The problem is that after five years of missteps, competitors are picking off Nike’s customers one category at a time. Runners who once swore by the Nike Pegasus are now lacing up Hokas, Ons, and Brooks. In fashion, it’s a similar story. Nike hasn’t produced anything to rival New Balance’s wildly popular 550s, or Adidas’s Sambas or Gazelles. And then there’s China. In June, the sportswear brand Li-Ning landed a 10-year deal with Steph Curry of the Golden State Warriors, a 12-time NBA all-star. It is arguably Li-Ning’s biggest endorsement contract since the brand signed Dwyane Wade in 2012, the year his Miami Heat won the NBA championship. Nike is trying to claw its way back. This week, the company announced its new Tuned Air technology, a high-tech evolution of the original Nike Air that will first make its way into an everyday running shoe. Next year, it hopes to generate about 10% of its revenue from products built on this innovation. But buzzy new shoe technologies will take Nike only so far in fixing its underlying problems. From the London marathon to the streets of Shanghai, Nike has lost both its innovation edge and its cool. The race is on to catch up on all fronts. How Nike Ceded Ground to Rivals Eight years ago, Nike opened a shrine to the swoosh on Manhattan’s Fifth Avenue. The House of Innovation rose six stories, wrapped in rippling glass. Inside sat the largest collection of Nike sneakers on earth. Staffers in white lab coats dip-dyed and embroidered shoes to order. Customers could reserve their shoes on the app, retrieve them from a basement locker, and pay on their phone. The store was dazzling. But looking back, it marked the moment Nike began to unravel. In 2017, the company unveiled a initiative to sell more of its products through its own stores, website, and app. After 50 years of carefully cultivating its relationship with retailers, Nike began cutting ties with many of the 30,000 stores that carried its products, including DSW, Dillard’s, Macy’s, and mom-and-pop shops that counted Nike as a major account. In 2020, Nike appointed a new CEO, John Donahoe, a former eBay chief with deep e-commerce experience, to accelerate this shift. The Nike House of Innovation, circa 2018 [Photo: Nike] The problem with this strategy was twofold. First, it cut off an key channel of communication between Nike and the retailers that best understood its customers, especially in the running and performance sectors. And it gave other brands the retail sunlight they needed to grow. Retailers suddenly had shelves to fill and lost revenue to make up. European upstarts like Hoka and On jumped at the chance to take Nike’s place. Adidas and New Balance expanded their real estate, helping turn vintage styles like the Samba and 550 into viral hits. “They all exploited this opportunity,” says Neil Saunders, retail analyst at GlobalData. “Smaller, more nimble players swiftly found ways to steal market share.” It took a while for Nike to realize how catastrophic the decision had been. During the pandemic, Nike’s customers had flocked to its website and app, helping it hit a record $50 billion in revenue in the fiscal 2023. But as soon as life returned to normal, shoppers in brick-and-mortar stores began discovering an exciting new selection of brands on shelves. By fiscal 2025, Nike’s sales had fallen to $46.3 billion. Hill, who took over as CEO two years ago, has been tasked with reversing the damage and winning back retailers. The brand is currently back in 30,000 stores. “We said that we would reset the marketplace, and that meant rebuilding our wholesale partnerships,” Hill told investors. The shift is showing up in the numbers. Last quarter, Nike’s wholesale revenue slipped just 1%, while its digital sales fell 13%. Its biggest launches now lean on retail partners. The Vomero 19 running shoe will hit more than 5,500 stores when it launches in March, and Nike looks to grow the footprint for its line of outdoor clothing and shoes, known as ACG, from about 3,000 doors to 8,000 by 2031, focusing on outdoor specialty stores. But getting back in the retailers’ good books won’t be easy. Many haven’t forgotten how abruptly Nike cut them off, and in the meantime, their shelves have filled up with a new generation of popular brands. “Dick’s isn’t prepared to give up space for Hoka, On, and other brands people like, just to suit Nike,” Saunders says. “Nike retreated, and it’s very difficult to regain the land you ceded from that retreat.” Sabastian Sawe of Team Kenya crosses the finish line at the 2026 TCS London Marathon, winning with a new world record time of 1:59:30 on April 26, 2026. [Photo: Alex Davidson/Getty Images] Nike lost its dominance in running After dominating the running shoe market for decades, Nike was overtaken by Brooks in 2022. Today, it’s in third place, after Hoka also pulled ahead. Many other brands, from On to Asics to Adidas, have been stealing market share by dropping new running shoes at a steady clip. “Nike allowed brands that were doing fresher things to come in and take business from them,” says Matt Powell, an analyst at the retail consultancy Spurwink River. These rivals benefited from Nike’s retreat from retail. But under Donahoe, Nike also pulled back on R&D. The former CEO made the controversial decision to reorganize product development around men, women, and kids, exploding the previous system of organizing innovation around sports like running, basketball, and soccer. One former employee characterized the move to Fast Company as “the biggest change in Nike’s history.” While the new structure was more efficient, it made for less innovative products. In 2023 and 2024, Nike didn’t release any new performance sneakers; it just made tweaks to existing models, like the Pegasus and Invincible. It was an abrupt and notable downfall for a company that arguably invented the modern running shoe. Nike is now trying to regain the ground it lost. Hill returned the company to its sports-focused organizational structure. “We’ve organized our teams cross-functionally around each sport, so we’re closer to the athletes, understand their needs and move faster to serve them,” Amy Montagne, president of the Nike brand, told investors this week. So far, things are looking up. Nike has had nine quarters of growth in running. The company wants to reclaim the top spot in running shoes priced above $100, and foresees more than $1 billion in additional running revenue between fiscal 2028 and 2031. Much of that will come from everyday runners’ choosing shoes like the Vomero. The Tuned Air technology, set to debut in a running shoe by late 2027, could hasten this trend. Analysts believes a comeback is possible. After all, brands like Asics and Brooks became major players in running after years of falling behind. But recovery takes time. “I do think we’re going to see better product and new ideas. Spring looks good and fall looks even better,” Powell says. “It takes years, in some cases, for a shoe to get to market. And, even then, one shoe is not going to change the fortunes of a brand of this size.” [Photo: Albo/Adobe Stock] Nike Lost Its Fashion Edge If you walk down the street, you’ll see millennial moms in retro New Balance runners, and teenagers in low-profile Adidas Sambas. Nike, once a brand beloved by sneakerheads, is getting harder to spot. “It’s a one-two punch of not being in stores and not being on people’s feet,” says Jeff Staple, the streetwear designer whose 2005 collaboration with Nike sparked riots. “It’s the classic problem of out of sight, out of mind.” Vintage sneakers are popular right now, and Nike has many in its arsenal. The issue is that the company hasn’t been strategic about how it rolls out classics. Under Donahoe, Nike identified bestsellers and then pumped them out, turning the Air Force 1, Air Jordan 1, Dunk, and Converse’s Chuck Taylor into multibillion-dollar franchises. By 2024, these sneakers alone brought in $13 billion, but the market quickly became oversaturated with them. People wait outside NikeTown London for a limited-edition Dunk release in 2007. [Photo: Gareth Cattermole/Getty Images for Nike] To clear the oversupply, Nike had to discount them, which is the kiss of death to a product’s popularity. In a 2024 profile in Fast Company, Donahoe stood by his decision to invest in these franchises. “We don’t apologize for exploiting the success of three of the largest franchises,” he said. Donahoe didn’t seem to understand fashion, Staples argues, which relies on delicately balancing supply and demand. Instead, Nike treated sneakers like commodities. “It comes from a very CPG [consumer packaged goods] mentality,” he says. “He treated these as numbers on a spreadsheet, without attaching any cultural nuance.” Emma Barratt, global executive creative director at the branding firm Wolff Olins, agrees with Staples: “The swoosh was everywhere, and it just lost its meaning.” Meanwhile, competitors like Adidas were more strategic about the release of new products. In 2024, when Adidas was gearing up to relaunch its Superstar sneaker, it cleared the market of existing shoes, so that the style would feel fresh. When it saw that the Samba and Gazelle were selling explosively, it constrained the supply of these shoes and used pricey limited-edition collabs, like the $350 Gazelle with Yohji Yamamoto, to keep them relevant. Nike’s leadership is now trying something similar. “We will continue to clear aged inventory out of the marketplace, recalibrate what we sell in, and be more disciplined in how we manage those franchises moving forward,” Hill told investors. These measures are necessary for “creating the foundation for profitable and sustainable growth,” he said. Creating scarcity is important, Staple says, but it is ultimately a short-term fix. Nike also needs to come up with fresher designs, not just rely on past hits. For instance, some of Nike’s recent wins among sneakerheads have remixed several vintage styles in unique ways. The Soulgoods x Nike Homescape Woven, for example, pairs a Nike Footscape-inspired woven upper with soles borrowed from other Nike models. “Nike needs to be more innovative, and not just in terms of making the fastest marathon shoes,” Staples says. “It also needs to make sneakers feel unfamiliar and fresh again.” Steph Curry of the Golden State Warriors in Li-Ning shoes, April 2026 [Photo: Eakin Howard/Getty Images] The China Threat When Curry announced in June that he was signing with the Chinese sportswear company Li-Ning (an endorsement and equity partnership deal estimated at $400 million over 10 years), it was the second time Nike had missed out on the NBA superstar. Curry began his career as a Nike athlete, but in 2013 he left for Under Armour. This year, Nike couldn’t—or wouldn’t—compete with Li-Ning. “Right now, China is probably Nike’s biggest problem,” says David Swartz, an analyst at Morningstar. Li-Ning and Anta, both founded in the early 1990s, have grown into powerhouse performance sportswear companies at home, and are increasingly competing abroad. (Anta has Klay Thompson and Kyrie Irving on its roster of NBA athletes.) That’s a problem for Nike, which generates more than half its revenue outside the U.S., including about 13% from China. “Local competitors are moving with speed and fluency,” Cathy Sparks, who took over Nike’s Greater China business in March, told investors this week. “Our marketplace and our model have not kept pace, and our results show it.” Nike’s revenue from the region—encompassing mainland China, Hong Kong, Macao, and Taiwan—fell 26% on a currency-neutral basis last quarter, and the company now expects sales there to stay roughly flat through fiscal 2031. Steph Curry attends a Li-Ning event in Tsim Sha Tsui, Hong Kong, on September 14, 2026. [Photo: Chen Yongnuo/China News Service/VCG/Getty Images] These Chinese brands are versed in Nike’s manufacturing playbook. Nike began partnering with factories in China in the ’90s, when the country was growing as a manufacturing hub. Nascent Chinese sneaker brands were able to tap into this shoemaking ecosystem to create products of similar style and quality. Decades later, these Chinese brands have grown so large they are now giving Nike a run for its money. Anta generated $11.6 billion last year, while Li-Ning hit $4.1 billion. (In a twist, Nike is now leaning on the same Chinese manufacturing ecosystem that helped Li-Ning and Anta catch up; Sparks tells me that Nike is working with local factories to develop premium materials at competitive prices.) To make incursions into the U.S. market, Li-Ning and Anta have taken another page from Nike by harnessing the star power of athletes. In 2012, Wade left the Jordan brand to sign with Li-Ning, eventually inking a lifetime deal with the brand in 2018 and creating his own line, Way of Wade. Thompson left Nike in 2014 to sign with Anta, which gave him a lifetime deal this year. In 2023, Anta brought on Irving to be its chief creative officer of basketball. That December, Nikola Jokić, the reigning NBA Finals MVP, left Nike for the Chinese brand 361°, which promised him his first signature shoe, something Nike had never given him. The Curry endorsement is the biggest signal yet of how far these brands have come. Nike is also losing ground among Chinese consumers. Its China revenue peaked in 2021 at $8.29 billion; by 2025, it had dropped to $6.59 billion. Its China market share dropped from 25% to 20% in that same time. Some of Nike’s problems in China are beyond its control, including youth unemployment, which is driving down sneaker sales, and a backlash against American brands for speaking out against forced labor in Xinjiang. But Nike also hasn’t done as much as its Chinese rivals to adapt to the nuances of the Chinese consumers, like creating styles tailored to their tastes. “Historically, Nike has exported American sports culture to the rest of the world,” says Morningstar’s Swartz. “In recent years, that model hasn’t worked as well in China, where Chinese consumers are more interested in buying uniquely Chinese products. Nike was slow to adapt to this.” Sparks agrees. When she worked in China 20 years ago, she says, Nike’s American identity “was certainly what helped us grow. But today it doesn’t give us the competitive advantage that it once did.” What matters now, she says, “is that we are locally connected to these consumers.” She has laid out a plan for Nike to start acting more like its Chinese rivals. The company is moving away from a model “centralized in Beaverton [Nike headquarters in Oregon] and executed through Shanghai,” and handing decisions to local teams in 20 Chinese cities, Sparks says. A new design team in Shanghai produced its first collection, 10 sportswear and Jordan styles, in under 120 days. Nike plans to double the team to more than 100 people by fiscal 2028, and eventually wants half the sportswear it sells in Greater China to be designed locally. “When you’re operating at our scale—still the number one brand in China with the highest consumer advocacy—those changes can’t happen overnight,” Sparks says. “But we are moving with a speed and commitment that we have not had in the past.”.

Rewind to the summer of 2016, back when Nike seemed unbeatable.

This spring, two London marathoners finally ran the race in under two hours—wearing Adidas shoes. A few months later, Adidas owned the FIFA World Cup, held in Nike’s backyard.
